en: Introduction: [Longqi] recalls Master Donggao Qianli.
I have said to myself that for many years I have been immersed in the vast winds of the Pure Land and the Sahā world;
yet even those such as Zhenru Zhe and Caotang Qing could not avoid occasional stumbles. He urged me to apply my mind diligently to this matter.
I happened to mention this to Master Bating, who already had a sub-commentary on the *Shizhi Nianfo Zhang* (Chapter on the Recitation of the Name of Amitābha by Śrī-Ābhāsvara) at his desk.
The two of us took up the volume and read it through together from beginning to end. We sighed in admiration, remarking that Mr.

Gao’s words—“to practice them with one's own body as medicine to save the age”—were indeed profound. Consequently, I instructed my son to solicit funds for its publication. Once the carving was completed, the Dharma... [text ends]

The Master further requested that I compose a preface for it. I considered that in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the Great Scripture, the Dharma-door of mindfulness of the Buddha was first proclaimed by the Bodhisattva Meghashri.
Maitreyanātha established the foundational treatises [of Yogācāra], wherein mindfulness of the Buddha and śamatha-vipaśyanā are held in equal importance.

Furthermore, while the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* is a work that discusses the nature (*dharmatā*), the chapter on Avalokiteśvara’s son Śrīkṣetra’s mindfulness of the Buddha is listed among the "Perfect Penetrations" (*avavādaka*) of the Chan school; thus, it cannot [be categorized solely as a discourse on the nature].
It is clear, moreover, that the Lotus School is not the path for returning to the source and seeing one's nature.

Currently, the *Commentary on the Amitābha Sūtra* and the *Pure Land Texts of Longshu* are widely circulated within the Chan monasteries; however, while the chapter on Avalokiteśvara is merely appended to the root sūtra, there has been no independent commentary dedicated to it.
Now, the Dharma Master has compiled this work by interpreting the text and elucidating its meaning, thereby adding one more [resource] for the people of China.

It is once again evident that [the practice of reciting the Buddha’s name] is a boat or raft for rebirth [in the Pure Land], and it cannot be said that it is not a meritorious contribution to the Pure Land.
Having thus conveyed this intention to Master Gao, I shall follow it with my own reflections. Master Tiantai said: "To recite the name of a single Buddha..."
This replaces those hundreds of thousands of millions of miscellaneous thoughts. Thought is itself emptiness; it is the manifest fundamental substance.
One does not attain Bodhi apart from thought. Furthermore, it is said: "When the holding of the Name reaches single-mindedness, one returns once more to the body of empty stillness.
It is also said: "One should know that the Pure Land is mind-only and has no external realm; one's own nature returns to its source."

The essence is the meaning of aspiring to be born in that land. Thus, although Master Padmasambhava advocated for the Western Pure Land with all his might, he did not neglect the fundamental principle of the Chan school regarding the realization of one's nature;

this is clearly evident. Therefore, it is not contradictory to say that the realization of one's nature is the ultimate destination of the Pure Land, while the Pure Land is the gateway to realizing one's nature.
As for the realization of one's nature, it is [to be free from] agitation...
The arms are all pure lands, yet the lotus pedestals themselves do not vanish. To say that one has not seen one's nature means that the pure land is not yet mastered;

however, the planting of the causal seeds must never regress. Thus, whether one has seen one's nature or not, both the recitation of the Buddha’s name and the cultivation of the pure land must not be neglected.
This principle seems to be what was not yet addressed in this chapter; I have therefore replied to your Highness accordingly.
I have thus recorded this in writing to verify for those who are truly able to practice the Buddha-remembrance (*nienfo*): what it is like to be such a person.
Written on the winter solstice of the Gengshen year of the Kangxi era by Dai Jingzeng of Qiantang.
[The Chapter on the Perfect Penetration of Buddha-Remembrance of Great Power Bodhisattva from the Śūraṅgama Sūtra of the Great Buddha-Crown]
Translated by the Indian Śramaṇa Prajñāmitra of the Tang Dynasty.
The Dharma Prince Mahāsthāmaprāpta, together with fifty-two bodhisattvas of his same rank, immediately rose from their seats,
prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
I recall that in the past, as many eons ago as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, a Buddha appeared in the world named Immeasurable Light (*Amitābha*).

Twelve Tathāgatas succeeded one another during that single eon, the last of whom was named Surpassing the Light of Sun and Moon (*Sūryacandraprabhāsa*). That Buddha taught me the Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha (*Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*).

It is like a person who is single-mindedly intent on remembering, and another person who is single-mindedly intent on forgetting; if these two people were to meet... [they would not recognize one another].
They meet; or perhaps they see one another, yet it is not a true seeing. These two remember each other, and their mutual remembrance is deep.
Thus it continues from birth to birth, like a form and its shadow, never diverging. The Tathāgatas of the ten directions cherish sentient beings as a mother remembers her child.

If the child has fled and wandered away, what can the mother’s remembrance do? But if the child remembers the mother as the mother remembers the child, then mother and child will pass through [the realms] together.
Birth is not far removed from non-contradiction. If sentient beings mindfully recollect the Buddha with their hearts, they will certainly see the Buddha in the present and in the future;

they will not be far from the Buddha. Without relying on expedient means, they will spontaneously attain the opening of the mind. It is like a person who has been perfumed with incense, whose body carries a fragrance;
this is called the Adornment of Fragrant Light. In my own stage of practice, I entered the state of non-arising by means of the mind that recollects the Buddha.
“Endurance! In this world, I gather those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha and lead them back to the Pure Land.

When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration of the faculties, I have no preference; I simply collect all six sense organs and maintain a continuous flow of pure mindfulness, thereby attaining samādhi.”
This is the first. (The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:

The Buddha told Ānanda, "If there should be another person who commits the four grave offenses and the ten *pārājika* transgressions, in an instant they will pass through this world and other worlds into the Avīci Hell, continuing until they have exhausted all the realms of uninterrupted suffering throughout the ten directions.")
Without having to undergo [retribution], one can, by means of a single thought, expound this Dharma-door to those who have not yet studied during the final kalpa.
The karmic obstacles of such a person shall be extinguished at that very moment; the causes for the suffering of hell they are destined to receive will be transformed into a Land of Peace and Bliss.
Thus, this chapter of the sutra is truly a great furnace for melting away sins, a divine elixir for curing illness, and a swift path for cultivating the mind.

This is the essential method for seeking birth [in a pure land]. If one can constantly maintain it, there is no suffering that will not be eliminated, no happiness that will not be granted, no wish that will not be fulfilled, and no fruit that will not be attained.
All who see or hear this should recite it three times over.
The Ritual for Daily Recitation:

(There are three classes of people. First, those who are entirely free from worldly affairs; they should maintain the recitation of the sutras and mindfulness of the Buddha throughout the six periods of day and night.
Second, those who are half-free and half-busy; they should single-mindedly maintain the recitation during the two periods of morning and evening each day.)
Third, for those who are extremely busy, they should single-mindedly recite [the mantra] once every morning. Regarding the procedure for recitation:
first, recite the name of the Original Teacher three times; next, recite the Chapter on Śrī-Ābhāsvara once; and finally, recite the *Wǎngshēng zhòu* (Sukhāvatī-vyūha Dhāraṇī) three times.
Recite the Verse of Praise for the Buddha once. Recite the names of the Buddhas one hundred, one thousand, or ten thousand times as desired.
Recite the names of each of the three Bodhisattvas ten times each. Finally, recite the Verse of Aspiration and Dedication once.

Before and after reciting, you must join your palms before a sacred image and perform three prostrations. If no Buddha image is available, perform the prostrations before the scripture or toward open space.

This is also acceptable. If one can indeed practice in this manner constantly and without interruption, the Buddha will surely take pity on them; whatever prayers or aspirations they may have, none shall fail to be fulfilled.
At the time of death, the Buddha and the assembly of sages will emit light to receive and guide them, leading them directly to rebirth in Sukhāvatī.

Practitioners should give rise to faith and aspiration; by no means should they harbor doubt or negligence. This clarifies that the daily recitation of the sutra and the invocation of the Buddha are to be performed together.

This is the proper method. For those who are extremely free from worldly distractions, apart from the six periods of daily recitation, they should practice mindfulness of the Buddha at every moment without interruption.
For those who are half-free and half-busy, they should practice mindfulness of the Buddha immediately upon finishing their affairs.
For those who are extremely busy, they should steal moments from their busyness to practice mindfulness of the Buddha even ten times; this is what is meant by not passing one's life in vain.
Throughout this entire life, if one does not abandon this for even a single moment, then the mind and mouth that recite the Buddha’s name will surely become the mind and mouth of a Buddha.

As the sutra says: "When one's practice is identical to that of the Buddha, one receives the Buddha’s spiritual influence, enters the lineage of the Tathāgata, and becomes a true son of the Buddha. Is it not so?
Homage to the Original Teacher Śākyamuni Buddha (recite three times).
(Next, following the section on Śrīkṣetra, recite the Mantra for Rebirth.
Namo amitābhāya (1) Tathāgatāya (2) Tadyathā (3) Amṛtodbhave (4) Amṛte (5) Siddhambhave (6) Amṛte (7)
(7) Vikaraṇḍe | (8) Amṛte | (9) Vikaraṇḍe | (10) Gamini | (11) Gaganā | (12) Citrakari | (13) Svāhā | (14) [The *Acintya-Ṛddhi-sūtra* states:
Regarding the method for reciting this mantra: purify the body and rinse the mouth; burn incense before the Buddha during the daytime.]
Recite it seven times for each of the six periods of the night; this can extinguish the sins of the five heinous acts and the slandering of the Dharma.
If one completes three hundred thousand recitations, one will immediately behold Amitābha Buddha. The *Commentary on the Amitābha Sūtra* states:
"If there are good sons or good daughters who are able to recite this mantra, Amitābha Buddha will constantly abide upon their crowns, protecting them day and night so that [no harm may come]."
Enemies will find no opportunity against them; they shall always enjoy peace and security in this life, and at the time of death, they will spontaneously be reborn [in the Pure Land].
Next, the verse in praise of the Buddha is recited:
The body of Amitābha Buddha is golden in color; His marks and signs and radiance are peerless.
His white tuft curls like five Mount Sumerus; His deep blue eyes are as clear as the four great oceans.
Within his light, countless billions of transformation Buddhas appear; The assembly of transformed Bodhisattvas is likewise boundless.
By the forty-eight vows, he delivers sentient beings, Causing those of the nine grades to all ascend to the other shore.
Namo Amitābha Buddha of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, the Greatly Compassionate and Greatly Merciful One (recite one hundred thousand, ten million, or more times as desired).
Namo Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva. Namo Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva.
Homage to the Bodhisattvas of the Pure Great Ocean Assembly (ten recitations each). (Then recite the verses for the dedication of merit and the making of vows.
I now invoke the name of Amitābha Buddha, whose true merits are real. I pray that you, out of compassion, will take me into your grace.
May you bear witness to my repentance and my aspirations. All the evil karma I have created in the past arose from beginningless greed...
All anger and delusion arising from my body, speech, and mind—I now repent them all.
May I, at the time when my life is about to end, be completely cleared of all obstacles and behold that Buddha Amitābha face-to-face, thereby attaining rebirth in the Land of Peace and Bliss.
By this merit, may I adorn the pure land of the Buddhas; above, may I repay the fourfold heavy debts of gratitude, and below...
To deliver beings from the sufferings of the three evil paths. May all who see or hear this give rise to the Bodhicitta;
throughout this present life, may they be reborn together in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. All Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time, all Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, Mahāprajñāpāramitā.
(Recite once. [At this point, one should kneel before the Buddha, recite each phrase while mindful, then rise and perform three prostrations before departing.]
(The verse says: "When impermanence arrives one day, Only then does one know they were but people in a dream.
Of the myriad things that cannot be taken away, Only karma follows along with the body. What are these myriad things that cannot be taken away?

Official rank, wealth and treasure, houses, fields and gardens, clothing and food and drink—even a beloved wife and cherished children—when impermanence arrives, none of these can be taken away. How so?

It is only karma that follows the person. Whether it be the evil karmas created by humans—such as greed, hatred, delusion, pride, the five heinous crimes, or the ten non-virtuous actions—or the virtuous karmas of precepts, concentration, wisdom, generosity, the five precepts, or the ten virtuous actions, when impermanence arrives, they all follow you closely.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "At the time of death, before warmth and sensation have departed, the good and evil deeds of one's entire life manifest all at once.

Those who are evil will immediately experience the retribution of suffering in the three miserable realms; those who are good will immediately experience the retribution of joy among humans and devas.

If within that wholesome mind there is also faith and aspiration, and one recites the Buddha’s name seeking rebirth [in the Pure Land], then the景象 (manifestations) of the realm of the Buddha of Ultimate Bliss will appear. The *Chapter on Vows and Practices* says: "This..."
At the time of a person’s death, all their faculties are utterly dispersed and destroyed; all kinsmen and relatives abandon them;
all power and influence completely fade away. Elephants, horses, carriages, precious treasures, and hidden hoards no longer follow along.
Only this King of Vows leads them from the front at all times, so that in a single instant, they attain rebirth in the Ultimate [Pure Land].
In the Land of Bliss, one beholds Amitābha Buddha and the assembly of holy beings.

Since this is so, why not exert yourself in diligent cultivation while you still possess this period of strength and health? Shandao said: "Even if gold and jade fill your halls, one cannot escape birth, old age, sickness, and death.
No matter how many kinds of pleasures you may enjoy, impermanence will inevitably arrive. There is only the direct path of cultivation."
Simply recite the name of Amitābha Buddha. Even if you wait until the moment of death to repent, what can be achieved by repenting afterward?
I exhort all people: practice and advance while there is still time. The matter of birth and death is great; impermanence is swift.
Be careful not to regard this as something beyond your capacity. Exert yourselves! Exert yourselves!
Furthermore, a person of pure karma prepares three provisions: first, faith. They believe that saṃsāra is most suffering; they believe that reciting the Buddha’s name is most sublime;

they believe that practicing in this land makes it difficult to achieve the fruit of the Path; they believe that by aspiring to be born in that land, one will certainly attain rebirth there even with ten recitations;
they believe that those born as humans or devas fall back once their merit is exhausted; and they believe that being reborn in the Land of Bliss for a single lifetime ensures one never regresses.

One shall subsequently attain perfect enlightenment. One should believe that reciting the Buddha’s name even once can extinguish the grave sins of birth and death accumulated over eighty billion kalpas;
one should believe that Amitābha Buddha embraces those who practice *nien-fo*, protecting them during illness and coming to welcome them at the end of life.

Second, one should make vows: may karmic obstacles be eliminated; may all sufferings be extinguished; may the mind be opened; may the Buddha be seen; may pure karma be perfected; and may [one] be born [in the Pure Land].

Repose in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang). Pray for the bestowal of prediction (vyākaraṇa). Pray for the deliverance of sentient beings. Third is practice: physically prostrating before the image, vocally reciting the name, and mentally visualizing—each must be single-minded and utterly free from distraction.

When one understands, realizes, and possesses faith and aspiration, it is the time when the lotus flower is planted. When one maintains focused mindfulness, it is the time when the lotus flower emerges from the water.
When the merit is perfected, it is the time when the lotus flower unfolds in the sky. Should one give rise to doubt or a regressive mind, the lotus...
The flowers have withered once more. From this point on, throughout the six periods of day and night, there shall not be a single thought of attachment to this Sahā world.
Whether rising or reclining, eating or dressing, speaking or remaining silent, moving or still, one must never forget the Pure Land.

When the time comes to end one's life, one should practice mindfulness of the Buddha and make vows; one must neither fear death nor crave life, but constantly reflect to oneself: "In my present body..."
Bound by suffering, impurities overflow. If one can cast this off, one will be reborn in a lotus pond and experience immeasurable bliss;
all matters will accord perfectly with one's wishes, like casting off foul, tattered rags and putting on precious, noble garments. Let go of all external conditions; body and mind are liberated.
At the mere onset of illness, regardless of its severity, one should immediately contemplate impermanence and wait for death with a single-minded focus. Thus—

I entrust this to all people: whenever anyone comes before me, they should recite the Buddha’s name for my sake; they must not engage in miscellaneous talk regarding worldly affairs, family matters, or the merits and demerits of others, nor cause further delay.
The Dharma Master should come frequently to admonish and encourage me, providing guidance according to the sutras.

When the time arrives that my illness becomes grave and I am about to relinquish this life, my family members and relatives must not weep or utter sounds of lamentation and distress; I fear that even this might [hinder my progress].
If the mind and spirit are deluded and distracted, causing one to lose right mindfulness, one should simply recite the name of Amitābha Buddha aloud and clearly.

One should maintain this until the breath ceases and the spirit departs; only then may one raise a lament. If one acts in this manner, there will be no doubt that among ten thousand attempts, ten thousand lives will surely lead to rebirth.

Furthermore, there are those who encounter obstacles and fail to attain rebirth through right mindfulness, such as those with hemiplegia who have lost the power of speech, or those who are insane and have lost their minds.

In the event of death by water, fire, lightning strike, being devoured by insects, beasts, or spirits, or dying from poison, in battle, or through the enmity of thieves and kings, one should likewise perform repentance in advance;

thus one will surely receive the protection of the Buddhas. For those who practice *nienfo* (recollection of the Buddha), there are six supreme benefits: first, they are protected and remembered by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
Amitābha dwells upon their crowns and emits light, while various heavenly deities and generals provide secret assistance day and night. Second, evil ghosts and poisons can do them no harm.

First, one will be able to harm [others]. Second, the three calamities and eight difficulties shall all be eliminated. Third, the obstacles of three lifetimes will be cleared like ice, enmities will be purified, and one will attain liberation from the cycle of birth and death.

Fourth, one’s vital strength will be full and complete, free from all sudden illnesses. Fifth, one’s dreams will be auspicious, and one will behold the physical forms of the Buddhas; no non-human spirits shall steal away one’s vital essence.
Sixth, one will be honored with prostrations by all in the present life, and at the moment of death, the Three Sages will come to receive and guide one. Thus it should be known.

To single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name in daily life is precisely to prepare for unforeseen contingencies. It is like a person entering a city on business who must first seek out a place to settle;
when evening falls and darkness descends, they will have a place to lodge. Seeking a dwelling beforehand is the preliminary cultivation of pure karma.
The arrival of evening and darkness is the coming of the great limit [of one's life]. Having a place to lodge—this is the Pure Land.

This means that one will be born within a lotus flower and encounter no obstacles or difficulties. If a person applies their mind in accordance with this, they will certainly attain rebirth at the time of death.
This, moreover, is the ultimate exhortation for those who cultivate the Pure Land.
*An Exhortation Composed by the Practitioner Xùfǎ of Cíyún and Xiāngyán:
Commentary on the Chapter on Śrī-Avalokiteśvara’s Perfect Penetration of Mindfulness of the Buddha from the Śūraṃgama Sūtra*, Fascicle One.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Guǎngdìng of Cíyún, Zhèjiāng, Qing Dynasty.
The commentary on this chapter is divided into three major sections. First, a general introduction to the overall significance; second, a detailed exposition of the underlying intent;
and third, a general introduction to the fundamental principles of the Buddha-remembrance (nienfo) school.
How magnificent is the Dharma-gate of *nien-fo* (Buddha-recollection)! It encompasses both the Great and the Small Vehicles; it gathers those of sharp and dull faculties alike.
Phenomena and principle are perfectly interfused; essence and appearance are without obstruction. The Buddha is this very mind—there is not a single moment of mind that is not the Buddha-mind.

This mind is the Buddha—there is not a single Buddha who is not the Buddha-mind. When the mind is recalled for a single instant, every Buddha is fully manifested; when a single Buddha is invoked, [the entire reality is revealed].
Mind and mind manifest simultaneously. There is no Buddha outside the mind that is recollected by the mind, nor is there a mind outside the Buddha that is praised by the Buddha.
When sentient beings recollect the Buddha, the Buddha is within the minds of sentient beings; when the Buddha recollects sentient beings, sentient beings are within the heart of the Buddha.
It is this mind that creates the Buddha; if the mind does not recollect, the Buddha is not created. Thus, the Buddha manifests the mind; it is not the Buddha who praises.

Yet, since the mind is not manifested [in other ways], we know that the single gate of *nien-fo* (Buddha-recollection) is truly the wondrous dharma for realizing one's nature and attaining Buddhahood.
The main section is divided into two parts; the first, the explanation, is further divided into two. First, a general clarification of its comprehensive inclusion. "Great indeed!
(*Da yi zai*) is a term of praise and also serves as an introductory phrase. "Nian" (recollection) and what follows are the dharmas being praised. The first phrase indicates the essence: *nien-fo*.

"Distinct" refers to the particular; "Dharma-gate" refers to the universal. The four phrases beginning with "Great" explain their characteristics. The first two phrases refer to persons. "Great" and "Small" are distinguished by way of vehicle (*yāna*);

"sharp" and "dull" are distinguished by way of faculty (*indriya*). "Collecting and encompassing all equally" means to transform and guide those of the Small Vehicle, turning them from the Small toward the Great.

Exert yourself to advance in the Mahāyāna; abandon the provisional to return to the real. Cause those of superior faculties to fully develop the three minds (first, the sincere mind; second, the profound mind;

third, the mind of dedication and aspiration) and enter directly into the non-arising [of phenomena]. Cause even those of inferior faculties to achieve success through ten recitations and likewise be born in that land.

The next two phrases concern the Dharma. Regarding practice, there is the unity of phenomenon and principle; regarding the truths, there is the unity of nature and characteristics. That these are perfectly interfused and unimpeded—even for those of the lowest ignorance—[is the intent].
Those who cling to phenomena are deluded regarding principle; those of limited wisdom grasp at principle while neglecting phenomena. Now, one must penetrate both principle and phenomenon.

By practicing in reliance on principle, one realizes the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) and beholds the self-nature of Amitābha; by practicing in reliance on phenomena, one realizes the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and is born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, the land of marks.
This is the section following the previous that specifically reveals non-duality within duality. First, the mind and the Buddha are non-dual.

The first four lines, based on the arising of the mind from its nature (*xingqi*), open up into five propositions concerning the relationship between the mind and the Buddha: 1. Outside the one mind there is the Buddha; outside the Buddha there is the mind. 2.
Within the one mind there is the Buddha; the Buddha is solely the mind. 3. The mind is itself the Buddha; the Buddha is itself the mind. 4. The mind is not the Buddha; the Buddha is not the mind. 5.
Mind and Buddha are perfectly interfused, without obstruction or hindrance. These five propositions are to be correlated, respectively, with the five teachings.
Understood. This now clarifies the meaning of the third phrase. This mind and Buddha encompass each other in their entirety, like gold and its vessels.
By means of the gold, the vessel is subsumed, leaving nothing of the vessel unaccounted for; by means of the vessel, the gold is gathered, with no part of the gold left out.

The first of the eight phrases concerning "mind" explains this through the perspective of cultivation. When the mind recollects the Buddha and the Buddha accords with the mind, both clearly manifest the nature of cultivation. When the mind recollects the Buddha...
It is manifested because the mind is itself Buddha; thus, Buddha is called the manifestation of mind. It is because Buddha is itself mind that the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) mind is recollected.
It is because there is no Buddha outside of mind that the unconditioned Buddha is so named. As the "Chapter on Dedication" (*Pariṇāmanā-parivarta*) of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:
"There is no suchness (tathatā) outside of wisdom that could be entered by wisdom, nor is there wisdom outside of suchness that could realize suchness."
This is precisely that meaning. "The three—sentient beings, the Buddha, and birth—are without distinction" means that there is no difference between the mind, the Buddha, and birth.
The first four lines correctly clarify this lack of distinction. Regarding "sentient beings recollecting the Buddha":

it is the sentient beings within the Buddhas' minds recollecting the Buddhas within their own minds. As for "the Buddha being within the sentient beings' minds," [it means that] outside of the sentient beings' minds, there is no further...

There is no separate Buddha, because the true mind of the Buddha is identical to the true mind of sentient beings. This clarifies that the Dharma is fully encompassed within the gate of the cause without exception. Therefore, it is said:
"If sentient beings bring mindfulness of the Buddha before them, they will certainly see the Buddha in the future. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* also says:
"One should know that in every thought-moment of one's own mind, there is always a Buddha attaining perfect enlightenment. Why is this? Because all Buddhas..."
Because the Tathāgata attains perfect enlightenment without departing from this mind. As for the Buddha’s mindfulness of sentient beings:
it is the Buddhas within the minds of sentient beings being mindful of the sentient beings within their own minds. Regarding those born within the Buddha’s mind:
outside the true mind of the Buddha, there are no further sentient beings, because the true mind of sentient beings is identical to the true mind of the Buddha. This clarifies the gate of fruition.
Thus, the Dharma is encompassed without omission. Therefore, it is said that the Tathāgatas of the ten directions cherish sentient beings as a mother remembers her child.
The *Buddhatva-śāstra* states: "All sentient beings are entirely within the wisdom of the Tathāgata;
because no sentient being can ever transcend the realm of Suchness (tathatā), they are all sustained and upheld by the Tathāgata. Based on this [pure]...

A Cool and Sparse Commentary on the Four Lines of Opening: 1. Outside the mind of the Buddhas, there are no other sentient beings. 2. Outside the mind of sentient beings, there are no other Buddhas. 3.

The arising of the Buddha-mind and the arising of the sentient-being-mind both exist and manifest simultaneously. 4. The minds of sentient beings and the minds of Buddhas mutually cancel each other out, resulting in the simultaneous disappearance of both.
For now, we shall clarify this by means of the first two lines. The four lines beginning with "This mind" follow upon the preceding [section].
This is revealed by contrast: the mind is fundamentally the Buddha; it is through non-awakening that the Buddha is obscured. If one wishes to become a Buddha, one must contemplate the mind.
The *Awakening of Faith* states that the fundamental awakening of sentient beings and the fundamental awakening of the Buddha are not two distinct entities.

If one does not contemplate the mind, it will be difficult to achieve Buddhahood. The Buddha is fundamentally the mind; it is because of ignorance that the mind is darkened. If one wishes to manifest [this luminosity]...
The mind must always be mindful of the Buddha. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states that the Buddha’s wisdom is vast and pervasive, encompassing the minds of all sentient beings;

the speech of sentient beings never departs from the Tathāgata’s wheel of Dharma. If one does not invoke the Buddha, it is difficult to clarify the mind. Thus, we know that what follows is the conclusion:
Amitābha is precisely one's own nature (*svabhāva*), and the Pure Land is entirely nothing but the single mind. Apart from the nature of the mind, there is nothing else.
Externally, there is nothing at all to be obtained. If one can maintain mindfulness, the Buddha of one's own nature will immediately manifest. The *Awakening of Faith* states:
"The single characteristic of the Dharma-realm is precisely the Tathāgata’s equal Dharmakāya. This is because once the Buddha of nature manifests, the Buddha of fruition is spontaneously realized.
Guishan said: "Now that you know the mind is the Buddha-mind, you will certainly become a Buddha. Is this not so? Even if...

It is like a sheep cart: the second vehicle, that of the *pratyekabuddha*, refers to the dharma-gate of dependent origination.
It carries sentient beings beyond the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) to dwell in the abode of cessation, thereby becoming a *pratyekabuddha*. It is like a deer cart:

the third vehicle, that of the Bodhisattva, refers to the dharma-gate of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*). It carries sentient beings beyond the realms of ordinary and small vehicles, proceeding directly to unsurpassed enlightenment.
It brings one across to the other shore of the Great Parinirvāṇa and accomplishes the fruit of Buddhahood, much like an ox-drawn carriage.

This present sutra belongs to the Mahāyāna, for it is through the Tathāgata’s compassionate regard for sentient beings, the empowerment of Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta to gather those who recite the Buddha’s name, and the establishment of peace and happiness for all vehicles that beings of the nine realms are delivered and liberated.
Regarding the five teachings: first is the Small Teaching (Hīnayāna), which speaks only of the emptiness of persons. Second—

First is the Initial Teaching (Shijiao), which clarifies only the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*); it is also called the Partial Teaching because it explains only the characteristics of phenomena (*lakṣaṇa*).

Third is the Final Teaching (Zhongjiao), which further teaches the Middle Way; it is also called the Real Teaching because it frequently discusses the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). Fourth is the Sudden Teaching (Dun jiao), which distinguishes only the true nature (*tathatā*).
Fifth is the Perfect Teaching (Yuan jiao), which speaks exclusively of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). This present sutra belongs to the latter three teachings.

The text below states: "Second, the depth of mindfulness: throughout successive lives, mother and child do not become estranged; at the end, as they gradually cultivate this mindfulness, they shall ultimately attain Buddhahood.

This refers to the Sudden [teaching]. It continues: "By means of the mind that recollects the Buddha, one enters the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) without relying on expedient means.

This is because one knows that the Buddha is identical to one's own mind, and thus swiftly achieves the Way of the Buddha. The text further states: "Completely gathering the six sense faculties, [one attains] purity..."
When mindfulness is continuous, one attains *samādhi*; this is "perfection" (*yuan*). Because one realizes that there is no distinction among the three [realms], one penetrates the Dharma-realm;
thus, it should be understood that the doctrine and meaning of this sutra are profound, vast, subtle, and far-reaching, rather than shallow or superficial. △ Third, the Essential Theme and Scope.
Regarding the three principles of the ultimate goal, there are both general and specific aspects. Generally, the principle is to recollect the Buddha and mindfulness of the Buddha;

the goal is the realization of the mind-ground’s perfect penetration upon seeing the Buddha and entering the stage of patience (*kṣānti*). Specifically, there are five pairs: first, teaching and meaning, where the teaching is taken as the principle.

1. Principles and Meaning: Taking the principles as the primary subject (*mūla*) and the realization of their meaning as the goal (*prayojana*). 2. Phenomena and Principle: Taking the manifestation of phenomena as the primary subject and the elucidation of the principle as the goal.

3. Object and Wisdom: Taking the three Buddha-objects as the primary subject and the two types of contemplative wisdom as the goal. 4. Practice and Stage: Taking faith, aspiration, and practice as the primary subject and entry into the stage of non-retrogression as the goal.
5. Cause and Fruit: Taking causal practice as the primary subject and the attainment of the virtues of the fruit as the goal.

The three phrases state the gateway; that is, they indicate the ultimate goal of the fundamental tenets. What the present sutra reveres is called the "tenet" (zong), and where the tenet leads is called the "goal" (qu).
If one does not recognize the tenet, there is no way to proceed toward the goal. The following section explains the meaning: "As for the teaching... and so forth.

This refers to the gateway of the Buddha’s teachings. "Thoroughly understanding the meaning" means to fully comprehend the meanings contained within the teachings regarding the objects and states of mind that are explained therein, as well as the principles of the mutual response between sentient beings and Buddhas, the entry into the stage of patience through the fragrance of cultivation, and the generation of lands by oneself and others.

Regarding what is contained within the meaning of phenomena and principle: this refers to the honoring of practices such as *nien-fo* (Buddha-recollection). What is the intent? It is precisely to manifest and clarify [these truths].
The Amitābha’s land of self-nature is the ultimate principle of mind-only. Regarding the opening of the realm and wisdom within the principle:

the "realm" is the principle that is the object of contemplation; "wisdom" is the mind that performs the contemplation. This is the true realm of the Buddha’s three perfect and harmonious bodies (*trikāya*).

"Single-mindedness in phenomena" and "single-mindedness in principle" constitute true contemplation. As for the arising of stages and positions according to wisdom, this refers to faith, aspiration, and practice.
These are the three provisions (*saṃbhāra*). Regarding "non-retrogression": when faith is pure and one is detached from the triple world, this is non-retrogression in status (*avasthā-avaivartika*).

When the mind aspires to see the Buddha and practices mindfulness of the Buddha, this is non-retrogression in aspiration (*praṇidhāna-avaivartika*). When one purifies conduct and gathers in those who follow the Buddha through the performance of wholesome deeds, this is non-retrogression in practice (*caryā-avaivartika*).

Furthermore, when faith in the transformative teachings of the Buddha transcends both mundane beings and external paths, this is non-retrogression in faith (*adhimukti-avaivartika*). When the aspiration to repay the Buddha’s grace transcends the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), this is non-retrogression in fruition.
Regarding the object (*viṣaya*): it is the non-retrogression of mindfulness. Regarding the practice of the Buddha-principle that transcends provisional cultivation and realization:

it is the non-retrogression of conduct. The *Commentary on the Awakening of Faith* states: "There are three stages. First, when the stage of faith (*śraddhā-caryā*) is not yet fulfilled, one is not yet called 'non-retrogressive';

however, because one dwells in conditions where there is no cause for retrogression, one is termed 'non-retrogressive. Second, from the fulfillment of faith onward, one enters the stage of the ten abidings (*daśa-vihāra*) and attains the vision of the Dharma-body."

Abiding in right concentration, it is called "non-retrogression. When the stages of the three or two worthies are fulfilled, one enters the first stage (*bhūmi*) and realizes the all-pervasive *dharmakāya*, being born in boundless Buddha-lands;
therefore, it is called "non-retrogression. Through faith, one achieves non-retrogression in faith;
through vows, one achieves abiding in non-retrogression; through practice, one achieves non-retrogression in the stages. The masters of the *Dilun* school say: "Abiding is realization."

"Regressing" refers to non-regression in position; "heading toward" refers to non-regression in practice; and "stages" refers to non-regression in mindfulness. Through faith, one achieves the realization of position;

through practice, one achieves the fulfillment of vows; and through mindfulness, one achieves the fulfillment of practice. That which is accomplished by the non-regression of cause and effect is as follows:
if the cause does not regress, it is called the true cause; if the fruit does not regress, it is called the true fruit. This is encompassed by faith, aspiration, and the Buddha-land.
Purity of the faculties and mindfulness are the causal practices for non-retrogression from bodhi.
Attaining the foremost perfect penetration of samādhi is the resultant virtue of non-retrogression from bodhi. The text has three layers: recollecting that Buddha is the cause;

the present and future vision of the Buddha is the result; mindfulness of seeing the Buddha nearby is the cause; the opening of the mind through the purification of fragrance is the result; and mindfulness of the mind [is the cause].
Entering into patience is the cause. Gathering people and returning them to the [Buddha-]land is the fruit. Thus, these five pairs function as causes for one another, giving rise to [the teaching].
△ Fourth, explaining the title.
Fourth, regarding the brief explanation of the title, there are four pairs of meanings. First is the general and the specific:

the three characters "Lengyan" (Śūraṅgama) constitute the general designation, as it applies universally to that entire great work; the seven characters beginning with "Shi" (Power) constitute the specific appellation, as they are restricted to this particular chapter.

Second, the teaching and its meaning. Within the aforementioned "individual" category, one distinguishes between the teaching and the meaning. That is to say, the single character *zhang* (chapter) is the teaching that expresses;
the six characters beginning with *shi* (power) are the meaning expressed. Third, the result and the cause. Within the aforementioned "meaning," this pair is further distinguished:
"perfect penetration" is the result, as it is the realized object; "power" and the others are the cause, as they are the contemplations that can be cultivated. Fourth, the person.
Regarding the Dharma: within the aforementioned causes, this pair is distinguished—the mindfulness of the Buddha is the Dharma received, and Śrī-Ābhāsvara (Potushe) is the person who propagates it.
These names are established based on these four paired meanings.

The first "four" indicates the heading; "there are" provides the explanation. This phrase lists [the categories]; the first "initial" explains them. Within the general [classification], there is also an implicit pairing.

The term *Lengyan* (Śūraṅgama) refers specifically to the meaning (*artha*); the term "sūtra" refers generally to the teaching (*śāsana*). The reason they are not explicitly stated here is as follows:
For fear of confusion and disorder: "The chapter belongs to the expressive" means that this is the chapter on the Buddha-remembrance teaching consisting of perfect and penetrating words and phrases.

It may be termed the correspondence between fruit and cause; it may also be termed the correspondence between object and wisdom—perfect penetration being the object and Buddha-remembrance being the wisdom.

It may also be termed the correspondence between the ultimate and the conventional, principle and phenomena, nature and cultivation, and tranquility and practice—perfect penetration being the ultimate truth, principle, and tranquil stillness. Its momentum...
This refers to the practice of recollecting the Buddha through mundane affairs. Regarding the four levels below:

those who recollect the Buddha recollect the *nirmāṇakāya* (the transformation body), not the *saṃbhogakāya* (the enjoyment body)—this is the "small" [level]. Those who recollect the *saṃbhogakāya*, not the *nirmāṇakāya*—this is the "end" [of self-retribution].

Those who recollect both the *nirmāṇakāya* and the *saṃbhogakāya*—this is the "beginning" [of other-retribution]. Those who recollect neither the *saṃbhogakāya* nor the *nirmāṇakāya*—this is the *dharmakāya* (the dharma body), which is the "sudden" [attainment]. Recollection...

The Buddha of Perfect Penetration and Non-obstruction (*Yuantong Wuzhang’ai Fó*). "Perfect" (*yuan*) refers to the ten bodies (*shishen*). Regarding the person of Shizhi: one who attains the power of the response-transformation Buddha (*yinghuafo*) is the Lesser Shizhi;
one who attains the power of the merit Buddha (*gongdefo*) is the Initial Shizhi; one who attains the power of the wisdom Buddha (*zhihuifo*) is the Final Shizhi (these two are retribution Buddhas);
one who attains the power of the suchness Buddha (*rirufo*) is the Dharma-body Buddha (*fahuo*); and one who attains the power of the inexhaustible Buddha (*wujin fo*) is the Sudden Shizhi.
(10 Buddhas) Perfect Avalokiteśvara. This is also a brief explanation according to the teaching; it will be explained in detail below.

Thus one knows that within this title, both person and dharma are manifested together, and cause and effect are presented side by side; the principle is exhausted and the meaning is complete, and so it is placed at the head of the chapter.
△ Fifth, the explanation of the text is divided into three parts. First, the description of the ritual for prostration and address.
The Dharma Prince Mahāsthāmaprāpta, together with fifty-two bodhisattvas of his same rank, immediately rose from their seats,
prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
[Commentary]: In the Sanskrit language, he is called Mahāsthāmaprāpta; here it is translated as "Great Power Attained. The *Siddhārthasāra-sūtra* states:
"Wherever I set my foot, the trichiliocosm and the palaces of Māra tremble; therefore, he is named Great Power Attained. The *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra* states:
"When this Bodhisattva walks, all the worlds of the ten directions tremble; when this Bodhisattva sits..."
At that time, the land of the seven treasures shook all at once. He is also named Mahāsthāmaprāpta. The *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states:
"I vow that my world shall be equal to that of Avalokiteśvara, without any difference. The Buddha Ratnagarbha said:
"Because you have made a vow to take up a great trichiliocosm, I shall now name you Mahāsthāmaprāpta; he is also named Anantaprabha. The *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra* states:
With the light of wisdom, he universally illumines all things, causing them to leave the three miserable realms and attain supreme power.

According to the original text, because he is able to cause one to mindfully recollect the Buddha of Great Power (Mahāsthāmaprāpta), able to restrain the delusions of the six sense faculties, and able to receive those who practice the mindfulness of the Buddha, he is named "Power-Attained" (Shizhi).
Using this Bodhisattva as the initiator serves to represent the Dharma-gate of mindfulness of the Buddha, which is capable of generating wisdom.
Light. Having attained great power, one leaves behind the suffering of the three realms and takes up the bliss of the pure land.

Being sovereign over the Dharma, one is called the Dharma King; being born through transformation from the Dharma, one is termed a son. The *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states: "In the past, during the causal stage..."
When Amitābha was a Universal Monarch (Cakravartin), Avalokiteśvara was his eldest son and Mahāsthāmaprāpta was his second son.

Now they reside in Sukhāvatī at the left and right of the Buddha, assisting in the transformation of all beings and destined to succeed him in the place of the Buddha; therefore, they are called "Dharma Princes" (Kumārabhūta).
"To be with" means to be of the same kind. It refers to the resonance of voice and spirit, which is called being of "the same class. "Fifty-two" is the number;

it represents the single gateway of the practice of mindfulness of Amitābha Buddha (*Śākyamuni*’s commentary on *Amitāyurdhyāna-sūtra*), for it can encompass the various dharmas and practices of the fifty-two stages, beginning with faith.
"Bodhisattva" is the full term for *bodhisattva*. Zao (Sengzhao) said: "Bodhi" is the name for the Buddha-way; *sattva*..."
In the language of Qin, it means "beings of great mind. Those who possess a great mind and enter the Buddha-way are called *bodhisattva*.
Xianxiu says: *bodhi* is here termed "awakening," and *sattva* is here termed "sentient being. Because they seek supreme awakening through wisdom, they are so named.
One who uses compassion to rescue sentient beings from below is called a Bodhisattva. Regarding "rising from one's seat":
the distinction between teacher and disciple, superior and inferior, is strictly observed; when there is something to report or petition, one should not remain seated.

Regarding "prostrating at the Buddha’s feet": placing one’s own crown upon the Buddha’s feet is the height of reverence. The above concerns the bodily action (*kāyakarman*). Regarding "addressing the Buddha": [this refers to the verbal action].

"Upper" (shàng) is indicated as "to announce" (gào); "lower" (xià) is initiated as "to inform" (bái). These belong to the karma of speech. Reverence through body and speech is thus established; the karma of mind can be understood accordingly.

[Commentary] "Fàn yǔ" (Sanskrit language) refers to the subsequent explanation of names. First, within the section on Śūraṃgama, the initial part concerns practice; the middle part cultivates one's own conduct.
Furthermore, because it possesses the power of wisdom and severance (*prahāṇa*), it can shake all things;

this is also called "the lower" [aspect], which refers to the vow to seek the Buddha-way above. Because it possesses the power of conceptualization (*saṃjñā*), it can realize and take hold of the Pure Land;

this is also called "the lower," which refers to compassion (*karuṇā*) that delivers sentient beings below. Because it possesses the power of transformation and guidance, it can rescue and deliver them.

The three paths [of rebirth]. The former two concern self-benefit; this one concerns benefiting others. According to the original text, the former applies universally to the explanation of names across various sutras, while this is restricted to the explanation within the present sutra.
The three phrases regarding "being able to recollect" are also explained in terms of the three meanings of seeking above, practicing in the middle, and delivering below.
As for the Buddha Mahāsthāmaprāpta, he refers to Amitābha; it is said that among the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time, [he is] Amitābha...

Because he is the foremost, he is able to bring others to mindfulness; unlike ordinary beings who do not seek the Buddha of Great Power nor the Dharma for severing suffering, he is able to gather them in;
unlike ordinary beings whose six sense faculties cling to the six objects of perception, he is able to receive them;
unlike ordinary beings who seek only their own benefit and cannot endure the prosperity of others, he possesses these three great virtues, which represent the ultimate extent of his majestic power.
The Bodhisattvas are named according to their true characteristics (*dharmatā*). It is known that sentient beings lack such power.
Among the Dharma heirs, those who are Dharma princes and exercise sovereignty as kings do so because "king" has the meaning of sovereignty.
Regarding those who succeed the Buddha: after Amitābha Buddha in that land, Avalokiteśvara shall next fill the position; after Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta shall then fill the position.

It is like a crown prince who temporarily resides in the Eastern Palace; later, he will surely face south to succeed to the royal throne. This is of the same category as the three [types of] "sharing" mentioned below.
The *I Ching* says: "Those of the same sound respond to one another; those of the same breath seek one another. Therefore, it is said that sound and breath correspond.

According to the *Avataṃsaka*, there are eighty-four similarities (ranging from "mindfulness-wisdom leading toward enlightenment" to "not departing in vain"), and for this reason they are called "similar types."
As in seventy-three [cases], these are not recorded here at length. Those whose paths differ do not plot together;
those who share the same heart find their fragrance like that of the orchid. Thus it is said, "to be of the same class. Five below, forty-five, forty-two. To believe in the Buddha is the mind.

To become a Buddha through faith encompasses the dharma-practice of the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*). To abide in samādhi and contemplate the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of the Buddha encompasses the dharma-practice of the ten abodes (*daśa-vihāra*).
To practice the conduct of mindfulness of the Buddha and deliver those who practice such mindfulness encompasses the dharma-practice of the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*).

Recalling the Buddha, the mind abides in the direction toward the Buddha; this encompasses the dharma-practice of the Ten Directions. Contemplating the Buddha within the ground of the mind, where the ground is like the ground of the Buddha;
this encompasses the dharma-practice of the Ten Grounds. Recalling the Buddha and mindful of the Buddha, one is not far from the Buddha;
this encompasses the dharma-practice of Equal Enlightenment. When the mind thinks of the Buddha, that very mind is the Buddha; this encompasses the dharma-practice of Wondrous Enlightenment. Thus...

To know that for transcending the mundane and entering the sacred, nothing is more wondrous than the recitation of the Buddha's name. Regarding "Bodhisattva" (*púxíà*): the first meaning concerns the mind;
it means that one who can thus remember the Buddha becomes a being of the Great Bodhi-mind and is therefore called a Bodhisattva.

Next, regarding the meaning in terms of the object: it is called a *bodhisattva* because one is able to seek the awakening of the Buddhas above with a mind of mindfulness of the Buddha, while transforming sentient beings below.
This explains the homage from the point of descending from one's seat;

the meaning is self-evident, for if the mind were not respectful, the body would not leave its seat and the mouth would not speak, as one performs physical and verbal prostrations to address the presiding master according to one's wish.

The reason why one cultivates reverence through all three types of action is to manifest that the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha is a dharma that is rare and difficult to believe in throughout all worlds.
△ Second, the formal presentation of what has been realized, divided into two parts. First, a detailed citation of ancient Buddhist teachings and admonitions, which is further divided into two.
First, a general clarification of the appearance of the Buddha.
I recall that in the past, during kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world named Immeasurable Light (*Amitābha*).
Twelve Tathāgatas succeeded one another for the duration of that kalpa, the last of whom was named Surpassing the Sun and Moon (*Sūryacandraprabhābhibhū*).
[Commentary] "I" refers to the Dharma-body itself; it is not the "self" as conceived by worldly sentiments. To clearly remember without forgetting is "recollection. "The past" is termed "bygone eras.
"Eons as numerous as the sands of the Ganges" refers to calculating eons based on the grains of sand in the Ganges River to manifest their extreme duration.
In Sanskrit, *buddha*; here it is translated as "the Awakened One," meaning one who awakens others from their lack of awakening.
Briefly, three meanings are opened up: first, self-awakening to the emptiness of the self (*ātman*), which distinguishes [the Buddha] from ordinary people and non-Buddhists;

second, awakening others to the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma*), which distinguishes [him] from those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*); third, awakening to the full emptiness of both [self and phenomena], which distinguishes [him] from bodhisattvas.

As for "one who has emerged from the world" (*lokottara*), there is no capacity for teaching that does not arise; he manifests when the faculties [of beings] have matured. As for "Tathāgata," it means arising from True Suchness (*tathatā*) and coming to achieve Perfect Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). Ten.
Second, the *Great Amitābha Sūtra* states: Buddha of Immeasurable Light; Buddha of Boundless Light; Buddha of Unobstructed Light; Buddha of Unrivaled Light;
Buddha of Flaming King Light; Buddha of Pure Light; Buddha of Joyful Light; Buddha of Wisdom Light; Buddha of Uninterrupted Light;
Buddha of Inconceivable Light; Buddha of Ineffable Light; Buddha who Surpasses the Light of the Sun and Moon. [There is no] Buddha of... [text ends].

"Measure" (mātra) means that true wisdom (*jñāna*) illuminates principle (*tattva*) without limit. "Boundless" means that expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) illuminates phenomena (*dharma*) without boundary.
"Unobstructed" means that the light of compassion bestows happiness without hindrance. "Without opposition" means that the light of pity (*karuṇā*) extracts suffering without adversary.
"Blazing King" means that the light-sound of transformation and response attains mastery. "Pure" means...
Because it emits radiance that is stainless and pure; because it brings great joy by causing others to experience its enjoyment;
because it is wisdom, for it destroys all delusions through great wisdom; because it is uninterrupted, for its constant light never ceases;
because it is inconceivable, for its fundamental light is beyond thought; and because it is inexpressible, for the surging light of a hundred jewels cannot be...
Regarding the term "surpassing the sun and moon": it means emitting all light to surpass the sun and moon. Regarding both being called "light":
in the causal stage, one contemplates the mind-light of the Buddha of Original Enlightenment; in the resultant stage, the Buddha of Wondrous Enlightenment manifests bodily light.
Regarding the twelve Tathāgatas succeeding one another for one kalpa: first, this refers to the capacity for contemplation, representing the twelve [stages] of the practitioner.
During this time, maintain pure mindfulness of the Buddha’s own nature in continuous succession, forging it into a single whole.
Do not allow even for the duration of a finger-snap a thought of the five worldly desires; then, immeasurable light of the nature will spontaneously manifest. Second, in terms of what is attained:
Thus, the twelve classes of beings are transformed into the twelve stages of sagehood, and the delusions of the twelve sense bases are transformed into the Buddha-virtues of the twelve sense bases.
However, these twelve Buddhas are ancient Tathāgatas, not the present Amitābha.

As for those whose names are identical, it is because the Way of teacher and disciple is one and the same, unchanged across antiquity and the present, such as in the case of Śākyamuni and Avalokiteśvara.

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "I" and so forth, this explains the two phrases "I" and "we. There are four types of "I": first, the false self of clinging views; second, the self of self and others...

1. The arrogant self; 2. The self of conceptualization; 3. The provisional self of names; 4. The true self of the Dharma-body. Worldly people possess false pride; those in training possess pride and the provisional;
the sages possess the provisional and the true. Now, Śākyamitra (Śrīmitra) is a Mahāsattva of the Dharma-body, unlike those of the three vehicles;
therefore, he possesses only the true self. The Ganges is also called the *Gaṅgā* River; this means "coming from heaven. The river flows from...
Because it comes from a high place, it flows out from the Anavatapta Lake. It is forty *li* wide, and its sand is as fine as flour.
When the Buddha was preaching the Dharma at Jetavana, this river was near the lecture hall; therefore, many things were said there, and it is taken as a metaphor.
In Sanskrit, *kalpa*; here it is translated as "differentiation of time. The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "The shortest unit of time is called a *kṣaṇa*; the longest unit of time is called a *kalpa*.
Here, the analogy of grains of sand is used for the *kalpa* so that the duration may be understood.

Regarding the six phrases beginning with "equality" (*samatā*) in the commentary on the Sanskrit text: the union of the beginning and the fundamental is termed "fulfillment of awakening" (*bodhiparipūri*). The total exhaustion of self and phenomena is termed...

Both are empty. [The passage] beginning with "The Great Amitābha" cites a scripture; that beginning with "Immeasurable" explains the meaning. The names of the various Buddhas differ in what they take as their realization:
some are causes, some are fruits; some are natures, some are marks; some are compassion and wisdom, some are vows and practices.

As for these twelve Buddhas whose names are derived from aspects of light, there are generally two kinds of light: first, the light of wisdom (*jñāna-prabhā*), and second, the light of the body (*kāya-prabhā*). Furthermore, there is...
There are two meanings: first, constant light; second, radiating light. Furthermore, there are two causes: first, the adornment of merit; second, the fulfillment of original vows.
Now, in explaining the name of the Buddha, we also rely on these six meanings. The first two relate to the two types of wisdom;
the third and fourth relate to the two minds, encompassing the two causes; and the fifth, sixth, seventh, and eighth relate to the four bodies. The fifth is...

The transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*). Sixth is the dharma body (*dharmakāya*). Seventh is the enjoyment body for others (*parasaṃbhogakāya*). Eighth is the enjoyment body for oneself (*svasaṃbhogakāya*).
These correspond to the *Lankavatara Sutra*'s Buddha of Response and Transformation, the Buddha of Suchness (*tathatā*), the Buddha of Merit, and the Buddha of Wisdom.
Ninth and tenth are the constant light and the emission of light. Regarding the "Buddha of Self-Nature," this refers to recollecting the Buddha of self-nature; one must not [recite] it.
Regarding the five desires, the *Contemplation Sūtra* states: "Those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha must not, for even the duration of a finger-snap, contemplate the five worldly desires.
This is called 'binding the mindfulness. If one can remain thus, without a single moment of distraction or intermingling, the immeasurable light of the Buddha’s own nature will [manifest]."

In the end, one attains illumination that transcends both the sun and the moon. As for the twelve classes of sentient beings, they are: those born from the womb, from eggs, from moisture, or by transformation; those with form and those without form;
those with perception, without perception, neither with nor without form, and neither with nor without perception.
As for the twelve stages of the sages, they are: Dry Wisdom, Faith, Abiding, Practice, Approaching, Heat, Summit, Patience, the Worldly First Dharma, the Grounds, and Equality.
Excellent. Regarding the absence of gradual stages, the Sūtra says: "From this, one practices gradually; according to what is initiated, one establishes the stages of the sages.
This is explained in detail in volumes seven and eight of the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*. As for the "twelve delusions," these refer to the delusions of the six sense organs and the six sense objects.
The Sūtra says: "The six disordered delusions constitute the nature of karma. The twelve divisions arise from...
