It is the same. "Remembering for a long time without forgetting" means that [the thought] remains in one's heart at all times;
even after passing through years and months, or until the end of one's life, it is not forgotten. "Joining the fingers" indicates the depth of mutual mindfulness. "Omitting the details" refers to...
This means that not only will one constantly behold the Buddha in this life, but even in future lives until the end of the future, one shall also constantly behold the Buddha.
"Contradiction" implies opposition; "difference" implies separation. Regarding form and shadow:

by briefly citing this single instance as an illustration of non-separation, it follows that sound and echo, water and waves, and the light of a mirror likewise never abandon one another. Furthermore, regarding these forms and shadows:

In relation to the proximate analogy below, the meaning of the text simply reveals the benefit of attaining the vision of the Buddha. In relation to the distant realization of the fruit below, the meaning of the text reveals both benefits:

attaining the vision of the Buddha (the first benefit, both present and future), and the opening of the mind through the fragrance of defilement (the second benefit). One should explain the text as follows:

"In this way, when one recollects the Buddha with a single mind, the mind becomes identical to the Buddha. When the mind is identical, the form is also identical; when the form is identical, [the essence is identical].
The same applies to the shadow. It is not only in this life; even throughout all successive lives, the form and the shadow remain identical. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:
"The appearance is like that of the Buddha, and the mental characteristics are likewise the same. When body and mind are united, one is called a Dharma Prince.
This is not the primary meaning of the opponent's position; therefore, the commentary does not explain it. 2. The Analogy of Mother and Child.
The Tathāgatas of the ten directions cherish sentient beings as a mother remembers her child. If the child flees and wanders away, what can the mother’s remembrance accomplish?
But if the child remembers the mother as the mother remembers him, then throughout successive lives, mother and child shall not be separated or distant.
[Commentary] The two preceding analogies referred generally to relatives and friends; thus, they were still somewhat broad and loose.

Therefore, this section again employs the analogy of mother and child—the most intimate of relationships—to cause people to give rise to faith and practice. Within this, there are also two parts. First is the analogy of being separated through mere remembrance;
the first three lines correspond to the first person who exclusively remembers [the other], while the following two lines correspond to the... [of the first].

Human beings are prone to forgetfulness. The Tathāgata is our mother, and all sentient beings are our children. In this world, there is no one whose compassionate concern is more urgent than that of a mother;
even if a child is rebellious, ungrateful, and unrighteous, a mother’s thoughts may waver, and she will feel regret and remorse in her heart.
The Buddha’s mindfulness of sentient beings exceeds that of a mother; toward those who are rebellious, evil, and grave in their offenses, the Buddha’s mindfulness becomes even deeper.
He even enters the Avīci Hell to undergo immeasurable suffering on behalf of these sentient beings.

Furthermore, a mother’s concern for her child is limited to a single lifetime, whereas the Buddha’s mindfulness of sentient beings is an inexhaustible heart of compassion that follows them through life after life without ever turning back. Therefore...
It is said that the Buddha’s mindfulness of sentient beings is like a mother’s remembrance of her child.
"If the child runs away" is a metaphor for sentient beings failing to mindfully recollect the Buddha and falling into the suffering of the evil realms. "Even though she remembers, what can she do?

is a metaphor for the Tathāgata’s solitary remembrance being of no benefit. "If the child... and so forth is a subsequent metaphor for the non-separation through mutual remembrance; the first two lines correspond to the aforementioned mutual remembrance.
The contemplation is profound. The final two lines mean that what arises and what gives rise to it are not different.

This refers to the way sentient beings of the six realms yearn for and contemplate the Tathāgata, just as the Tathāgata compassionately contemplates sentient beings; only then do the paths of response and invocation intersect, such that the living being and the Buddha are non-dual.
Therefore, the Great Master Da Xing of the High Qi dynasty said: "The four characters of 'Buddha-remembrance' (nianfo) are the core of our veneration and the teaching we proclaim."

This means that the two characters "faith" (xin) and "mindfulness" (yi) are never separated from the mind, while the two characters "veneration" (cheng) and "respect" (jing) are never separated from the mouth.
Whether at will or at dawn or dusk, there shall never again be a dwelling in the Sahā world. This is the foremost essential strategy for the practice of *nienfo*.
[Commentary] Regarding the term "generally": this includes all teachers and disciples, as well as sovereigns and subjects. [The text says] "As for the Tathāgatas... and so forth. Question:

The previous statement said that when one recites the Buddha's name, one recites only Amitābha and not the Buddhas of the other directions; why then does this passage speak of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions? Answer:

There are two interpretations. First, it refers specifically to the single Buddha Amitābha, because throughout the three periods of time and the ten directions, there are immeasurable Buddhas named Amitābha.

The *Contemplation Sūtra* states that from the Sukhāvatī of the Golden Light Buddha in the lower direction, up to the realm of the King of Radiance Buddha in the upper direction, within this interval, there are infinite manifestations of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, as numerous as the atoms of countless worlds. Second, it refers generally to...

This refers to the Buddhas of the ten directions. It means that it is not only I, Amitābha Buddha alone, whose compassionate vows are thus; rather, the compassionate mindfulness of all Buddhas of the ten directions is likewise the same.
This clearly demonstrates that the Way of every Buddha is identical. Thus, the "Chapter on Questions and Clarifications" in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:
"The Tathāgatas of the ten directions share one and the same Dharma-body; they possess one mind and one wisdom, as well as [the ten] powers and [the four] fearlessnesses."
It is likewise so. The fourth fascicle of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "All Buddhas possess four kinds of equality:
namely, equality of letters, equality of speech, equality of body, and equality of Dharma. The *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra* states: "Those who behold the Buddha Amitāyus..."
One immediately beholds the infinite Buddhas of the ten directions who look upon one with compassion. The *Samādhi Sūtra* states: "The mind of all Buddhas is great compassion.
That which is the object of this compassion is suffering sentient beings. When one sees sentient beings undergoing suffering and affliction, it is as if an arrow has pierced one's heart;
one desires to extract that suffering. Therefore, those who seek rebirth [in the Pure Land] must not engage in [discursive] contemplation.

If you harbor evil thoughts and doubt that the Buddha will not come to receive you, who knows that the Buddha’s heart is solely intent on saving sentient beings who suffer against their will through various means?
Why do you allow yourself to give rise to such doubts and obstacles, willingly accepting a miserable rebirth? Question:
Is there a difference between these two lines regarding "fleeing" and the previous meaning of "forgetting whether one meets him or not"? Answer: They are both the same and different.
Regarding "the same": if one does not bring the Buddha to mind, one cannot see the Buddha; even if one sees the Buddha, one will not receive the benefit of the Dharma.
This is no different from fleeing away. What is the use of recollecting others? Regarding "the different": this refers to the meaning of the previous analogy.
It clarifies that while sentient beings may at times bring [the Buddha] to mind, they do so without urgency and without deep recollection; therefore, it is as if they had never encountered him.

"Even upon meeting [the Buddha], it is still beneficial to remember him. The intended meaning of this metaphor is that sentient beings not only forget their mindfulness, but furthermore slander the Buddha;
because they do not believe, they fall into the three miserable realms and undergo immeasurable suffering.

Therefore, if one flees away, remembering the Buddha will be of no benefit. Regarding the generation of the Buddha through resonance: the child is a metaphor for the "generation," and the mother is the "resonance."

This is a metaphor for the Buddha’s response. "The Way intersects as non-dual" means that they merge without contradiction. Therefore, the high aligns with the low. That treatise states: "To be reborn in the Pure Land, one must possess faith.
If one has faith in a thousand [names], one will be born a thousand times; if one has faith in ten thousand, one will be born ten thousand times.
If one does not depart from the Buddha’s name in thought and speech, all Buddhas will immediately rescue and protect one. One should constantly keep the Buddha in mind."
To constantly recite the Name with the mouth and always show reverence with the body is what is called "deep faith. II. Harmonizing with the Dharma:
If sentient beings, in their minds, recollect the Buddha and think of the Buddha, they will certainly see the Buddha in the present and in the future.
[Commentary: "The mind of sentient beings" distinguishes this from oral recitation where the mind does not attend. "Recollection" (*smṛti*) means to remember, to hold in mind, and not to forget.
"Mindfulness" (*manasikāra*) means to bind the object of focus within one's heart. Furthermore, at the initial stage, when one briefly exerts effort to retain a memory, it is called "recollection.

At a later stage, when the object is familiarized over a long duration and mindfulness flows spontaneously, it is called "mindfulness. Moreover, "recollection" refers to a temporary, single instance of remembering; "mindfulness" is...
"Recollection" (*anusmṛti*) refers to constant mindfulness. If one recollects phenomena (*dharma*), one focuses the mind with single-minded attention, free from all distracting conditions.
If one recollects principle (*tattva*), it is solely the wondrous, enlightened clarity that perfectly illumines the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). There are also two aspects of the Buddha:

first, the aspect of phenomena (*nimitta*), which consists of the three bodies (*trikāya*) and ten bodies; second, the aspect of principle (*tattva*), which is solely the single, true Dharma-realm. Furthermore, regarding phenomena and principle...
Within the mindfulness of the Buddhas, there are again two aspects each: first, sequential arrangement (*pratipātya*), and second, perfect interpenetration (*yuganaddha*).

This means that one first recollects the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and the reward body (*saṃbhogakāya*), and subsequently the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) and so forth; this is the sequence of phenomena. If three or ten [bodies] are simultaneously present within a single mind, this is the simultaneity of phenomena.
First emptiness, next non-emptiness, and finally both emptiness and non-emptiness; this is the sequence of principle. These three are as follows...
The *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness) and the Buddha are contemplated as being co-present at one and the same time; this is the principle of perfect interfusion (*yuanrong*). Question:

If there is a Buddha external to the mind, how can one contemplate them as being identical? If there is no Buddha external to the mind, what is the use of ritual practice (*shiwèi*)? Answer: There is a Buddha external to the mind.

Regarding the Buddha: through the Buddha within my own mind, one realizes that external Buddha. As the sutra says, "The true knowledge of all Buddhas arises from the mind’s conception"; therefore, one must practice mental recollection (*li-nian*).
That there is no Buddha outside the mind means that by relying upon the external Buddha, one reveals the Buddha within my own mind.

As the sutra says, "When one conceives of the Buddha with the mind, it is this very mind that creates the Buddha"; therefore, one must practice objective recollection (*shi-nian*). If one were to depart from these two modes of recollection—both the objective and the mental—[the path would be lost].
"What is meant by 'this very mind is Buddha'? Question: "If Buddha is precisely this mind, one should simply be mindful of the mind; why must one be mindful of Buddha?
Furthermore, if this very mind is Buddha, one should simply be mindful of Buddha; why must one be mindful of the mind? Answer:

"It is merely that you cling to the idea that 'Buddha is the mind,' yet you do not realize that my own inherently enlightened mind-nature (*prakṛti-pratibhāsa-citta*) is that ultimately enlightened Buddha. As the Sūtra says: [This is...]"
The mind is itself the Buddha with the thirty-two marks; therefore, it does not preclude the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha.

Furthermore, while one may hold that the mind is itself the Buddha, one must not fail to realize that this very Buddha of ultimate awakening is one’s own original awakened nature (prakṛti). As the Sūtra says: "All Buddhas enter into the hearts of sentient beings.
Therefore, it does not preclude the practice of mindfulness of the mind. If one were to focus exclusively on either the mind or the Buddha, the meaning would not be established.
Question: The single true Dharma-realm is in essence devoid of dual characteristics. Why, then, do notions of "internal" and "external," or "mind" and "Buddha," persist?

Answer: The single truth of the Dharma-realm is fundamentally without internal or external; it does not belong to the Buddha-mind. Yet, the Buddha, through his own exhaustive realization, knows that these exist within all sentient beings.
To cause awakening to arise, the meaning is divided into mind and Buddha: the Buddha is taken as the external object, and the mind as the internal object.
When the merit of mindfulness is perfected, one realizes this spontaneously: there is no mind outside of the Buddha, and no Buddha outside of the mind.

There is only the single Dharma-realm, universally fused and inexhaustible. Those who see the Buddha before them do so without departing from their present aggregates, within meditative concentration.

One sees [the Buddha]. Or one may see him within a dream. As for "those who shall see the Buddha in the future," this refers to seeing the Buddha come to welcome them at the end of their retribution when the *skandhas* (aggregates) perish;

or it refers to seeing him within a flower. Regarding the statement that this is "certain," there are two meanings. First, because the mutual resonance between the practitioner and the Buddha is inconceivable.
That is to say, having attained faith that the mind itself is the Buddha, one focuses single-mindedly on the affairs of practice, moment after moment.

Because of one's devotion to the Buddha, one perceives the *vipākaphala-buddha* (the Buddha as the fruition) entering into the center of one’s own mind. As the Sūtra says: "This mind creates the Buddha.

The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, enter into the conceptualizations of all sentient beings. This is because the beginning and the fundamental nature are in accord; it is the very nature of reality (*dharmatā*).

That is to say, through faith one realizes that this very mind is the Buddha, and by focusing exclusively on the principle, one contemplates the Buddha of the original nature within oneself. Regarding this self...
Within the mind, one perceives the manifestation of the Dharmakāya Buddha. As the Sūtra says: "This mind is the Buddha.

When one contemplates the Buddha with the mind, this very mind is the thirty-two marks. In this context, it is not that the Buddha recollects sentient beings; rather, the emphasis lies on sentient beings recollecting the Buddha.

[Commentary] Regarding "recollection" (*smṛti*) below: the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* asks, "What is recollection? Its nature is to cause the mind to clearly remember and not forget objects previously experienced;
its function is to serve as the basis for meditative concentration (*samādhi*). That is to say, it repeatedly recalls and maintains objects previously perceived, ensuring they are not lost."
Because it can induce meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one does not give rise to any recollection whatsoever regarding objects or categories of entities never before experienced;

even regarding those previously experienced, one cannot clearly remember them, and thus mindfulness (*smṛti*) does not arise. As the Master of Repentance Ciyun said: "Whenever one encounters and engages with various conditions and affairs..."
Yet, not forgetting the Buddha within one's inner mind is called "recollection" (anusmṛti). It is like when worldly people have their minds bound by urgent matters;

even while engaging in various activities such as speaking, coming and going, sitting, lying down, and performing tasks, they do not hinder the secret recollection of previous events, which remains vividly present.
The mind that recollects the Buddha should be likewise. Should one ever lose mindfulness, one must repeatedly collect and restore it.

After a long time, this becomes one's nature; one spontaneously and constantly recollects [the Buddha]. Furthermore, if a subtle evil thought arises in the mind, one immediately recollects the Buddha.
By the power of the Buddha, the evil thought naturally subsides. If one sees others suffering, with a mind that recollects the Buddha—

Have compassion for them and vow that they may be free from suffering. By continuing in this manner, mindfulness of the Buddha and the binding of the mind to it can accomplish all the merits of the Pure Land.

As for the "inferior practice," this refers here to single-minded recollection, as well as the inferior "gathering of the faculties" and "pure mindfulness"—that is, the "single-mindedness without confusion" and "exclusive and constant mindfulness" of the *Amitābha Sūtra*, and the "binding the single mind" of the *Contemplation Sūtra*.

This is mindfulness (*smṛti*). It encompasses both phenomena (*dharma*) and principle (*li*). Regarding phenomena, the subject and object of perception are clearly distinguished within the mind as the Buddha;

there is only this single thought-moment, with no other thoughts, continuing in uninterrupted succession to accomplish the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). This is what *The Awakening of Faith* means when it says that through the causal conditions of single-mindedly recollecting the Buddha, one achieves this.
Regarding principle, the subject and object are of one suchness; the mind and the Buddha are non-dual. There is only this one...

Conditioned by this, there are no other conditions; the mind is sovereign over its conditions, and the power of wisdom is perfected. To give rise to faith means that although one is mindful, there is neither a subject who can mind nor an object that can be minded.
Furthermore, the *Pumen shu* states: "If one applies the mind to maintain mindfulness without interruption, it is called 'single-mindedness in practice' (*shi yixin*).
If one realizes that the four natures of this mindful mind do not arise, it is called 'single-mindedness in principle' (*li yixin*)."

Regarding the mind: within each of the four or five preceding modes of mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*), both these aspects of phenomenon (*dharma*) and principle (*li*) are fully present. Question:
Do the four or five gates mentioned previously and these aspects of phenomenon and principle differ in meaning, or are they both defined by the subject who practices mindfulness?

Answer: The four or five gates previously mentioned indicate that there are many skillful means (*upāya*) for designating the Dharma-gates; these aspects of phenomenon and principle, however, are defined according to the practitioner’s application.

The minds are distinct. Therefore, within the four or five gates, two minds must necessarily be present; and within those two minds, the four or five [factors] must necessarily be subsumed. There is no confusion or overlap. Question:
Regarding the phenomena (事) and principle (理) herein, how does this differ from the previous judgment of phenomena and principle regarding the four or five forms of mindfulness of the Buddha?
Answer: In the former case, the four and five gates were judged separately, with each belonging exclusively to either phenomena or principle. Herein, however, it is comprehensive.
Regarding the judgment that both the four, five, one, and one [teachings] possess both principle (*li*) and phenomena (*shi*), when compared, the former is brief while the latter is detailed;

thus, they are not the same. Nevertheless, within these two types of mindfulness, although neither may be omitted, there are those of superior intelligence who focus exclusively on the mindfulness of principle, those of dull faculties who focus exclusively on the mindfulness of phenomena, and those of middling capacity who practice both principle and phenomena according to their respective dispositions. All of these accord with the suitability of the individual's capacity.

There is no need for hesitation or obstruction, as the benefit of being able to see the Buddha is the same [for all]. Furthermore, the Buddha also descended [to ask]: "Among the three [bodies], the Dharma-body;
and among the ten [aspects], the wisdom-emptiness body and so forth—why are these also called 'phenomena' (*vastu*)? Answer:

Because they fall within the realm of numerical calculation (the number thirty), and because they belong to the Buddha’s body (the phenomena of bodily marks). Question: The *Awakening of Faith* states: "If a person single-mindedly recollects Amitābha Buddha..."
If one practices the roots of goodness, one immediately attains the vision of the Buddha; is this not the contemplation of phenomena (*dharma-smṛtyupasthāna*)? Furthermore, it is said:

"If one contemplates that Buddha’s *tathatā* dharma-body and constantly and diligently practices it, one will ultimately attain birth [therein]"; is this not the contemplation of principle (*tattva-smṛtyupasthāna*)? Why, then, would the dharma not belong to the category of principle here? Answer:

In the treatise, because it refers to the *saṃbhoga-kāya* and *nirmāṇa-kāya*, it belongs to the contemplation of phenomena. Now, however, because it refers to the single true reality (*ekasatya*), it is likewise...

Regarding the subject matter: this is why the *Mañjuśrī-prajñā* clarifies the single-practice *nien-fo samādhi* by first elucidating such concepts as the immovable dharma-realm and the dharma-realm that binds conditions.
The *Great Commentary* (*Dà shǔ*) also states: "Since even the practice of the single dharma-realm is itself non-existent."
Question: The Buddha of the Ten Bodies appears exclusively in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* and is not found elsewhere; why, then, is one instructed to recollect him in the present teaching? Answer:
Although the teachings spoken by the various Buddhas differ, the thirty bodies are common to them all. Thus, the *Contemplation Sūtra* states: "The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, are the Dharma-realm body.
This is just as Meghashri (De Yun) did when he recollected the Buddha of the Ten Bodies. The *Qingliang Shuchao* also says: "However..."

Regarding this *nien-fo* samādhi, its general characteristic is one, while its specific aspects consist of the three bodies (*trikāya*) and the ten bodies; the cultivation of contemplation for each is distinct.

As for the three bodies, they refer to the contemplation of the Dharma-body, the Reward-body, and the Transformation-body. Within these three bodies, each has both the primary (the body) and the secondary (the environment), which together constitute six contemplations.

That is to say: contemplating the Dharma-nature as the body and the land constitutes the primary and secondary aspects of the Dharma-body; contemplating the Flower Treasury World (*Huazang*) and so forth constitutes the Reward-body.

The buddha-fields serve as the support for the [buddha-]body. The ocean of marks and signs of the ten bodies (*daśakāyalakṣaṇasamudra*) and so forth constitute the primary [body]. Recollecting the pure lands, the water-birds, and the forest trees constitutes the support for the emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
The thirty-two major marks and so forth constitute the primary [body] of the emanation body. As for the "ten bodies," they are:

the body of recollection, the body of vows, the body of wisdom, the body of the power of dharmas, the body of sustaining, the body of mental transformation, the body of miraculous power, the body of majesty, the body of awakening, and the body adorned with the marks and signs of merit. As it is said:

This constitutes the realm of the Indra’s Net of multiple layers; it is the gateway to Samantabhadra’s practice of Buddha-recollection (*buddhānusmṛti*). This is detailed in the sixty-second fascicle.

It involves both the sequential progression of practice (*pratipatti-krama*) and the perfect fusion within a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa-samantabheda*). Those of sharp faculties attain through perfect fusion, while those of inferior dullness proceed through sequential stages.

For those of middling faculties, there is no fixed rule. Furthermore, those of sharp faculties may first realize the principle (*li*) and subsequently engage in phenomena (*shi*), whereas those of dull faculties [may do otherwise].

The principle of subsequent order is entirely according to circumstances and lacks any fixed characteristic. Regarding the phrase "first, emptiness, etc.," this is provisionally based on the *Four-Volume [Treatise]* concerning the Illumination of the Tathāgata-garbha Mind within our own school.
If one were to correlate this with the Dharma-realm within the principle of what is contemplated, it should be stated as follows:
first, the Buddha of the unconditioned principle-Dharma-realm; second, the Buddha of the conditioned phenomenon-Dharma-realm; and finally, the non-obstruction of principle and phenomenon.
The Buddha of the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu-buddha). Because the Tathāgatagarbha of the Dharma-realm is of one mind, it is merely a matter of different expressions for the same thing.

First, the question addresses a potential objection regarding the two types of mindfulness: the difficulty that one need not possess both, as either may be employed according to need. Second, the question addresses the difficulty regarding the identity of mind and Buddha:
the point that when mindful of one, the other is necessarily present, so they do not need to be pursued simultaneously. Third, the question addresses the identity of mind and Buddha.

Regarding the difficulty of maintaining both the perfected mind and the Buddha simultaneously: as for those who see [the Buddha] within meditative concentration, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* (Chapter 46) states:
"If there are sentient beings who single-mindedly recollect and keep [the Buddha] in mind, then the Buddha will appear before them," and so forth. Chapter 62 states:

"By abiding in the gate of mindfulness of the Buddha through the mind of mastery, the Buddha’s image appears according to the inclinations of one's own mind. Furthermore, regarding the gate of mindfulness of the Buddha by abiding in all objects, it is universally...
Because one perceives the manifestation of the Buddha within all objects, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "The Buddhas possess two kinds of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*):

first, causing [beings] to enter samādhi; second, manifesting their bodies to bestow empowerment. Because Bodhisattvas and others receive these two empowerments, they are able to personally behold all Buddhas.
The *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra* states: "The marks, signs, and radiance of Amitāyus Buddha pervade the ten directions."
Because the Buddha encompasses and does not abandon those sentient beings who mindfully recollect him, they are able to see him within meditative contemplation (*dhyāna*).
As for seeing him in dreams, the *Lotus Sūtra* states: "If, in a dream, one sees the Tathāgatas sitting upon lion thrones, surrounded by assemblies as they preach the Dharma.

Furthermore, the text on the "Lower Grade" of rebirth in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* says: "When such a person approaches the end of life, they will see that Buddha in a dream, and shall likewise attain rebirth there."
Regarding those who are born [in the Pure Land] and see the Buddha at the end of their retribution:

the *Sūtra on the Praise of the Merits of All Buddhas* states, "If there are those who hear the name of Amitābha and believe and rejoice with a single mind, when such persons reach the end of their lives, Amitābha Buddha will stand before them."
The *Drum-Sound King Sūtra* (*Gongyinwang jing*) states:

"If there are those who uphold the name of that Buddha, at the time of their death, Amitābha Buddha will immediately appear before that person together with a great assembly, causing them to behold him.

Regarding those who behold him within a flower, the text on the middle grade of the lower class in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* (*Guānjing*) says: "He blows various celestial flowers, and upon each flower are transformation Buddhas and Bodhisattvas."
Upon welcoming this person, they are born within a lotus flower in the space of a single thought-moment. It takes six kalpas for the lotus flower to open;

during that time, Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta preach the sūtras to them. Question: Now there are those who single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name, yet do not see the Buddha even in their settled dreams.
Furthermore, there are those who recite the Buddha’s name throughout their entire lives, yet at the time of death, they are not reborn in the Pure Land. Why is this?

Why is this? Answer: If one focuses the mind single-mindedly on the Buddha yet does not see him in dreams, it is because their past karmic obstructions are heavy and their present power of goodness is weak.
Furthermore, the Buddha has two ways of bestowing grace: first, when there are no obstructions, he grants manifest grace, causing one to see him directly;
second, when obstructions are heavy, he grants hidden grace, allowing one to receive benefit in secret. Thus, Samantabhadra...
It is said: "There are sentient beings who, within their hearts, manifest the practice of Samantabhadra. At that time, I manifest my body in various forms and arrive at each of their locations.
Even if their obstructions are so deep that they do not yet see me, I secretly place my hand upon their heads and provide protection so that they may succeed.
As for those who recite the Buddha’s name but fail to be reborn in the Pure Land, it is because their recitation lacks sincerity and they harbor doubts."
Because they lack firm faith; because they lack the vow for rebirth there; and because they are unable to sever craving and attachment. Question:

While present roots of goodness may be shallow and thus capable of being increased through cultivation, how can one know that past karmic obstructions are deep and heavy so as to apply their respective remedies?
Answer: There are two ways to distinguish this. First, if within samādhi there arises a sign of the emergence of roots of goodness.
Thus one knows that in the past one planted the causes for goodness. What constitutes the manifestation of this goodness? Briefly stated, there are four kinds.

First, regarding the manifestation of the roots of goodness of the Transformation Buddha (*nirmāṇa-buddha*): within the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*, one suddenly recollects the Buddha and cultivates the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) and the myriad practices, thereby accomplishing the thirty-two marks (*dvātriṃśan-lakṣaṇa*).
The body possesses a sublime radiance, the mind possesses wisdom, and one preaches the Dharma to benefit sentient beings.
Subduing the enmity of Māra, when one gives rise to such thoughts, a heart of reverence and love is born; samādhi is awakened and the practice of the Buddha is advanced.
Either within meditative concentration, one perceives the physical marks of the Buddha’s body and attains pure faith and understanding;

or within a dream, one hears the Buddha preaching the Dharma and awakens to the Buddha-mind. Regarding the signs of the arising of roots of goodness as a recompense for these two types of mindfulness, at the time of recollecting the Buddha:
Suddenly, one recollects the Buddha’s body of perfect fruition, which is entirely accomplished through untainted merit (*anāsrava-guṇa*).
Each of its marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) and its radiance is immeasurable; its supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) fill the entire *dharmadhātu*.

This continuity remains serene and tranquil until the end of the future. When one contemplates in this way, the understanding of wisdom becomes clear, the mind of concentration is secure, and wholesome thoughts arise.
Continued: Or, while in meditative concentration, upon hearing an exposition of the inconceivable realm of the Buddha-dharma, one immediately gives rise to immeasurable gateways of wisdom.
Or, within a dream, upon seeing the eighty-four thousand exquisite marks and signs of excellence, one immediately gives rise to immeasurable merit from vows and practices.
Regarding the manifestation of the roots of goodness for recollecting the Dharma and the Buddha: at that time—
At the time of samādhi, one suddenly recollects the Buddha’s true reality-body (*dharmakāya*), which is pure and signless like empty space;
it is solely the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), devoid of the realm of conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*).

It is free from arising and free from ceasing, unconditioned and uncreated, neither coming nor going, neither decreasing nor increasing. When one forms this thought, the wholesome mind unfolds and one enters meditative concentration.
At peace and blissful, they penetrate immeasurable Dharma-gates and manifest boundless Buddha-realms.

Or, while in meditative concentration, they see the Buddha with the subtle and wondrous Dharma-body endowed with all the marks and signs; they then immediately awaken and remain far removed from both permanence and impermanence.

Yet, it manifests as both permanent and impermanent. The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "The Dharmakāya has the five dharmas as its nature; it is not that the pure Dharma-dhātu alone is called the Dharmakāya.
When one awakens in this way, the samādhi of actual wisdom is revealed and manifests before one, or perhaps within a dream.
Upon seeing that the Buddha takes the reality of all phenomena (*dharmatā*) as his body, one immediately attains awakening.
Taking True Suchness (*tathatā*) as the Buddha, there is no realm that is not the Buddha. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The suchness of all phenomena is the true mark;
this suchness of all phenomena is itself the Buddha. Apart from this, there is no other Buddha. When one awakens in this way, the six sense faculties become pure.
The nature manifests before one. Regarding the signs of the arising of the roots of goodness of the ten Buddhas of the four mindfulnesses:

within meditative contemplation, one suddenly recollects the Buddha’s body-cloud of the Dharma-realm, in which the environment and its inhabitants are perfectly interfused, the true and the responsive are unimpeded, the one and the many enter into each other, the large and the small are hidden and manifest, and it is both principle and phenomenon, both person and dharma, both this and that, and both cause and fruit. Furthermore...
The nine realms are also the Buddha-realm; they are also the three bodies and the ten bodies.

When one contemplates in this way, the inexhaustible mind of goodness is opened and developed, inexhaustible samādhis are produced, the layered afflictions are extinguished, and the layered dharma-nature is revealed.

Or, within meditative concentration, one may see unobstructed Buddha-fields, manifesting bodies and preaching the Dharma within every atom of those lands. Thereupon, one immediately attains realization.

Having thus understood that from the single gate of mindfulness of the Buddha within the Cloud of Virtue arise twenty-one gates, one should thereafter give rise to the vows of Samantabhadra and practice the conduct of Samantabhadra.
Alternatively, within dreams, one may see infinite manifestations of the Buddha preaching the Dharma and benefiting sentient beings.

Even if one enters the Samādhi of Buddha-Recollection of Majestic Radiance and masters the infinite samādhis, after such awakening, one gives rise to the wisdom of Vairocana and accomplishes the realm of Vairocana.
All these superior roots of goodness are the manifestations of the retributive causes (*vipāka-hetu*) from past and present lives of recollecting the Buddha.

(Seeing all the marks and signs [of a Buddha] belongs to the manifestation of the retributive cause; the arising of various wholesome minds is entirely the emergence of the habituating cause [*vāsanā-hetu*]). This is the second [point].
If, within this state of mental dullness, signs of the arousal of karmic obstacles appear, one knows that one did not plant roots of goodness in the past. What constitutes the arousal of obstacles?
This is also divided into four types. The first is the sign of the arousal of karmic obstacles characterized by torpor and obscuration; this refers to when one is recollecting the Buddha.
First, even when one is in deep sleep, in a state of profound darkness and mental fog, there is no discernment, which prevents various meditative contemplations from being developed.
Second, the manifestation of the karmic obstacle of distracted discursive thought: when wishing to practice contemplation, although one is not in a state of dullness, [discursive thoughts arise].
One gives rise to false conceptions, desiring to commit the four grave offenses, the five heinous crimes, the ten evil deeds, and acts of violating the precepts;

these continue in succession without ceasing for even a moment. Because of this, the samādhi cannot manifest before one. Third is the manifestation of karmic obstacles arising from the pressure of adverse conditions:
when about to enter meditative absorption, although there are no deluded thoughts, adverse conditions appear, such as seeing [one's body] being burned.
They may drown; or they may hear thunderous crashes; or they may be headless or handless; or they may fall into mountains and seas.

Thus oppressed, they are made to feel alarm and terror, so that the resolve for the Way which they have generated is obstructed and fails to arise. Fourth is the manifestation of the karmic obstruction of the suffering of illness:
when one is mindful of the Buddha, although there is no supreme object [of focus], the body suddenly develops various diseases and afflictions.
In a hundred ways, one may be entangled in various worldly affairs without interruption; because of this, one cannot realize the Unborn.
These aforementioned karmic obstacles are all manifestations of the retributive causes of past unwholesome deeds.
By observing the manifestations arising from these two dharmas—good and evil—one can verify whether one’s own faculty-nature is wholesome or unwholesome, and thus know for oneself.

Having observed whether, in a previous life, one planted roots of merit or failed to plant them, and whether one committed evil deeds or refrained from them, one should further cultivate and bring to perfection those that are good, and apply remedies to eliminate those that are evil. How are they to be remedied and eliminated?
This is also explained through four gates. First, to remedy and eliminate the obstacle of dullness (*styāna*), one should be taught to recollect the thirty-two marks of the transformation Buddha.
From among these marks, select one; for instance, take the mark of the white tuft of hair (*ūrṇā-kośa*) and observe it with eyes closed.
If the mind is dull and dark such that visualization fails to arise, you should face the dignified and majestic form of a Buddha and take that as your object to enter meditative observation.
If it is not clear, then open your eyes to look, and then close them again. When visualizing in this manner, the eye of the mind will open wide and clearly, and [the veil] will be pierced.
This obstacle is the absence of deep sleep. Second, to remedy and eliminate the obstacle of discursive thoughts,
one should be taught to recollect the Buddha’s ten powers, four fearlessnesses, eighteen unique qualities, samādhis, liberations, inconceivable and immeasurable merits,
the benefits of his universally manifested form-body, and all his supernatural powers and transformations.
Subduing the Māras and externalists: by thus recollecting the merit of the Buddha’s wholesome dharmas, all evil states of mind and mental factors will naturally be extinguished.
Third, as for the subduing and extinguishing of obstacles consisting of evil objects, one should be taught to recollect the Dharma-Buddha. As for the Dharma-Buddha:
This is precisely the equal *dharmatā*, empty, quiescent, and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). It has no form or characteristics.
Since it lacks form and characteristics, how could there be the oppression of objective spheres (*viṣaya*)? Because objective spheres are empty, this is the remedy that extinguishes these hindrances.

Fourth, regarding the remedial extinction of the hindrance of the affairs of illness, one should be taught to recollect the ten Buddhas, sustained by the majestic power and the merit of their original vows derived from the Bodhi of the Buddhas.
They are not entangled by worldly affairs. Contemplating the marks and signs of the Buddha’s merit—the adorned body born of mind—they are not afflicted by any suffering of illness.
They contemplate the Buddha’s Dharma-body as being like space; according to their power of wisdom, they manifest transformations for all beings.
This is not like the body of sentient beings, composed of the aggregates of affliction, which is tormented by the eight sufferings and worldly matters.
It is like being bound by cocoons, as if a silkworm has no day of emergence. When one contemplates in this way, these obstacles are immediately extinguished.

Thus, one should know that if one maintains the mind in mindfulness of the Buddha, there is no vast merit that will not be accomplished, and no deeply heavy karmic obstacle that will not be extinguished.
Question: When mindfulness of the Buddha causes the Buddha to appear, can there also be demons? Furthermore, regarding the roots of goodness generated through mindfulness of the Buddha...

"Is there the presence of Māra or not? He replied: "The Buddha possesses the power of supernatural penetrations (*abhijñā*), the power of majestic virtue (*tejas*), and the power of his original vows.

Within his great radiance, there can certainly be no demonic interference (*mārakarma*). However, if one's past obstacles (*pūrvāvaraṇa*) are profound or if one applies the mind improperly, it is possible for Māra to arise;
this must be discerned. The sūtras and śāstras distinguish two cases: first, when the manifested marks and signs do not accord with the sūtras."
These are the works of Māra. Second, not being in accord with what one originally practiced is the work of Māra.

Regarding the signs of the arising of roots of goodness, there are two types of discernment as to whether they are the work of Māra or not the work of Māra. First, regarding the mind and its objects, and the duration or speed [of their arising]:
if these matters—such as seeing the Buddha or hearing the Dharma—are the arising of roots of goodness, then they are the retributive cause.
The appearance of the objective field manifests for a brief moment and then vanishes, while the causal continuity of the cultivated wholesome mind remains uninterrupted.
If this were produced by Māra, then the appearance of the objective field as a retributive cause would not cease for a long time; it might vanish and then return again to cause disturbance.

The cultivated wholesome mind, having arisen briefly, would then perish, or it might suddenly transform into an evil thought. Second, [the distinction] is based on the lightness or heaviness of the afflictions.

This means that when one perceives auspicious signs arising, they can cause the mind and consciousness to become agitated and disturbed, increase the weight of afflictions (*kleśa*), create numerous obstacles, and be detrimental to the concentrated mind;

all such instances belong to the deeds of Māra. However, if one perceives auspicious signs appearing, even if one has not yet realized meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), the body and mind become bright and pure, wholesome thoughts are awakened, afflictions become slight, or samādhi may open up.
Body and mind are joyful; internally and externally one is at peace; the complexion is radiant and moist; afflictions are stilled;
and merit is sublime—these are the signs of a successful commencement. If one has not yet distinguished between the false and the true, one should employ two methods as antidotes:
first, the method of cessation (*śamatha*), which means entering deeply into samādhi and single-mindedly recollecting the Buddha regarding the manifested signs.
Know them all to be empty and deceptive; simply abide in equanimity and concentration, neither grasping nor rejecting.

When the mind is thus stilled and silent, and no further discrimination arises—if these are the realms of the sages, then the power of concentration will grow ever deeper and the auspicious signs will accord with the Dharma.
If they are the manifestations of demonic realms, they will naturally collapse before long; even if they appear, they will not accord with the Dharma. Second is the contemplation of dharmas.

This means contemplating the true emptiness of the *dharmadhātu* and recollecting the Buddha of the Dharma of Space. By investigating and examining manifest appearances, one finds no place of their arising.

Because appearances are empty and quiescent, the mental recollection is likewise quiescent. Knowing that the suchness (*tathatā*) of the realm of Māra is identical to the suchness of the realm of the Buddha, one realizes that apart from *tathatā*, there is not a single dharma-characteristic.
Through such contemplation and recollection, the Buddha-dharma will naturally manifest before one, and the realms of Māra will spontaneously vanish.
[They] are extinguished. However, for one who practices mindfulness of the Buddha (*nien-fo*) to encounter a demon is a case of one in ten thousand.

This is truly because a person who cultivates the karma of the Pure Land possesses three powers: first, the power of mindfulness; second, the power of the intrinsically existing Buddha-nature; and third, the power of the Buddha’s grasping and protection (*parigraha*).
How, then, could malevolent demons find an opportunity to disturb or harm them? Thus, the *Sūtra on the Praise of the Merits of All Buddhas* states: "If..."
If there are those who hear the name of Amitābha, Amitābha Buddha will stand before that person; Māra cannot destroy their mind of right awakening.
For this reason, one should simply practice mindfulness of the Buddha with a single mind and harbor no doubts.
The phrase "it is certain" (必定) serves to resolve such difficulties. An objection is raised: "The Tathāgata comes from nowhere and goes nowhere."
How is it that a Buddha appears before one? Therefore, this text explains in general that there are two reasons why one will certainly see the Buddha.

First, regarding other Buddhas—meaning the True Buddha of the Dharmakāya, which is fundamentally without birth or extinction. From this Truth, the response-body (nirmāṇakāya) arises; thus, coming and going do not hinder its manifestation.
For this reason, when the mind is pure, the Buddha appears; when the mind is defiled, the Buddha vanishes. It is just like the moon appearing when the water is clear.

"When the water is turbid, the moon is lost. Second, this is explained in terms of the Buddha within oneself—that is, the Buddha of the originally enlightened mind (*mūla-āśraya-buddha*). Essentially, there is no coming or going;

yet, depending on whether one is awakened or unawakened to that enlightenment, appearing and disappearing are not obstructed. Therefore, when the mind is deluded, the Buddha is hidden; when the mind is awakened, the Buddha is manifest. This is like the dust and light of a mirror:
when the mirror is clean, its radiance shines forth. The following section also serves to resolve doubts. An objection is raised: "The above..."
In the second analogy, both contain the Tathāgata’s mindfulness of sentient beings. Why, then, is it said that there is no mindfulness of sentient beings within?
Therefore, it is explained here: "Because sentient beings lack faith and aspiration. This is a repeated contemplation and exhortation;
that the Buddha is mindful of sentient beings is his own original vow—what need is there for words? △ Second, the realization of the fruit, in two parts. First, the explanation by way of Dharma.
Not far from the Buddha, without relying on expedient means, one spontaneously attains the opening of the mind.
[Commentary] The first phrase refers back to the previously explained cultivation of causes; the subsequent two phrases correctly clarify the characteristics of realizing the fruit.

Regarding "not distant": in present observation, when observing another Buddha through the mode of objective recollection (*vastu-smṛti*), one first perceives the Buddha of the form-body (*rūpakāya*) and subsequently the true Buddha of the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).

When observing one's own Buddha through the mode of conceptual recollection (*dharma-smṛti*), one first perceives the Buddha of partial realization and subsequently the Buddha of ultimate realization.
In future observation, when observing another Buddha through the mode of objective recollection, one first perceives the nirmāṇakāya Buddha and subsequently the saṃbhogakāya Buddha.
When one perceives the Buddha within one's own nature, there is first the Buddha of Original Enlightenment (*mūla-ādi-bodhi*) and subsequently the Buddha of Sublime Enlightenment (*prakarṣa-bodhi*);

therefore, it is said that "the Buddha is not far away. Regarding the phrase "without relying on expedient means": in terms of phenomena (*dharma*), the practice of *nien-fo* (Buddha-recollection) is itself the supreme and extraordinary expedient;
why rely on other gates of expedient means to assist in manifesting one's own original nature? In terms of principle (*li*), Buddha-recollection is itself...

Contemplate the mind. The mind and the Buddha are without difference; self and other are non-dual. How could one depart from the Buddha that is one's own mind and rely upon an external Buddha as a provisional means?

For those who have personally attained the opening of the mind, they enter the Buddha’s knowledge and realization through the mind of nianfo (buddha-recollection), thereby perfecting bodhi and returning to the state of non-attainment.
In terms of phenomena, this is the realization of the fruit of Buddhahood; in terms of principle, it is...
The essence of awakening is perfectly manifest; what one attains is simply the vision of Amitābha. This is why there is no need to worry about failing to attain enlightenment.
[Commentary] The first phrase provides a brief summary, while "not far" and following provide a detailed explanation. Regarding the phrase "manifest before one," an objection is raised:
"Since one has already seen the Buddha above, why is it now said that he is 'not far'? Therefore, this explanation states: "The vision of the Buddha mentioned above..."
This is precisely the fundamental source from which form is differentiated. This future Buddha is the ultimate realization of the Dharma and the wondrous fruition of retribution;
therefore, they are not mutually exclusive. Furthermore, because one perceives the Buddha, sentient beings and the Buddha exist in the same place, like a form and its shadow.
It is not contradictory or remote. △ Second, the explanation by way of analogy:
It is like a person who has been perfumed with incense; their body possesses a fragrant scent. This is what is called "adornment with the light of fragrance."
[Commentary] The first two phrases present a simile. The Dharma-body within [the practitioner] is close to the Buddha’s body, and their mind opens to the Buddha’s mind.
This corresponds to the person in the simile who, having been anointed with fragrance, has their own body also become fragrant. The next two phrases state the name [of the practice]:

that is, to adorn one’s own mind—the *tathāgata* of original enlightenment—with the fragrance and light of the *tathāgata*’s Dharma-body. It is like the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, which uses sandalwood and aloeswood incense.

The preceding [passage] used the incense of the bodhicitta as a metaphor; here, the fragrant incense of humans and devas is likewise used as a metaphor for the fragrance of the merits of the Tathāgata’s Dharmakāya.

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "the Dharma above and below": if one speaks directly in terms of the Dharma, it refers to the "fragrant incense" of mindfulness of the Buddha, which brings one near to the fragrance of the Buddha’s body. This opens [the meaning].
The "incense of the Buddha-mind" is precisely what the Elder Vāsava (the Perfumer) refers to as the "incense of generating the mind to recollect the Buddha.

This is illustrated by the following analogy from the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra*: "Just as worldly garments have no fragrance in themselves, yet they come to possess a fragrant scent through being perfumed by incense, so too the defiled dharmas of ignorance have no pure karma in themselves;
it is only through being perfumed by True Suchness (*tathatā*) that they become pure."
Because of habitual practice, there is the function of purification. As for the defilement of ignorance, the originally awakened mind—the Buddha-store—is within the shell of ignorance.
That treatise clarifies the Tathāgata-garbha while still enmeshed in afflictions; this sutra uses a metaphor for the Tathāgata-garbha that has emerged from its entanglements.

Therefore, it is said that "the mind opens. This means that the opening of the mind constitutes the attainment of Buddhahood because one is near to the Buddha. It is like how the body becomes fragrant through the application of incense.

If one were to formulate a syllogism according to the *lakṣaṇa* school (Sautrāntika), it should be stated as follows: "The recollection of the Buddha" is the subject (*dharmin*). "The opening of the Buddha’s mind" is the thesis (*sādhya*).

The reason (*hetu*) is: "because one is not far from the Buddha. The concordant example (*sapakṣadṛṣṭānta*) is: "like a person who has been perfumed by incense. Here, "the person who has been perfumed" is the subject.
The body is adorned with fragrant light; the reason given is "because of being perfumed. The "common analogy" is like mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*).
"Emerging from" refers to emerging from samādhi, and it is also the name of a dharma-gate. As stated in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, fascicle 78:
"Just as white sandalwood, when applied to the body, can remove the heat of affliction and bring about coolness, so too is the fragrance of the bodhicitta."
It can eliminate the burning afflictions of greed, hatred, and delusion, causing one to be endowed with the coolness of wisdom. Furthermore, it is like the black sandalwood incense of the heavens:
if even a single *zhu* is burned, its fragrance pervades a thousand worlds. So too does the fragrance of the bodhicitta;
the merit of a single thought universally perfumes the entire Dharma-realm. Moreover, a Wheel-Turning King possesses a precious agalloch wood called "Elephant Treasury" (*hastigarbha*). If...
When this incense is burned, the King’s fourfold army all ascends into the void.
When the incense of the bodhicitta is ignited even once, it causes all roots of goodness to forever transcend the triple world.
Furthermore, just as the fragrance of the bark of the pārijātaka tree cannot be matched by any other floral scent, so too is the great vow issued from the tree of the bodhicitta.
The fragrance of merit cannot be matched by the fivefold Dharma-fragrance of all those of the two vehicles (*dvayāyānika*).
Furthermore, while the *pāri* flower perfumes a garment for a single day, the *campaka* and other such flowers, though perfumed for a thousand years, cannot equal it.
The fragrance of the flowers of the bodhicitta, perfumed throughout a single lifetime, surpasses all fragrances of merit and all the untainted merits (*anāsrava-guṇa*) of the two vehicles. (100)
Even those perfumed for a thousand kalpas cannot equal it. Regarding the fragrance of humans and devas, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:

"In the human realm there is a fragrance called 'Elephant Treasury' (*hastigarbha*), which arises from the combat of dragons. If one pellet is burned, it rains down fragrance for seven days; and if anyone comes into contact with it..."
All become golden in color. Any sentient being who smells it will experience seven days of happiness and freedom from all illness.
From Mount Malaya comes sandalwood incense called "Ox-head" (Gośīrṣa); if it is applied to the body, fire cannot burn it.
In the ocean there is an incense called "Invincible" (Anabhibhūta); if it is applied to conch shells or drums, when their sound is emitted, the enemy forces will all retreat. A...
On the banks of Lake Nairañjanā grows the agallochum known as Padmagarbha;

if one pellet is burned, its fragrance pervades Jambudvīpa, and those who smell it are freed from transgressions and their moral precepts become pure. On the Snowy Mountains there is a fragrance called Aruṇa;
whoever smells it is liberated from all defilements. In the realm of the rākṣasas, there is a fragrance called Sāgaragarbha, [which belongs to] the wheel-turning monarch.
At the time of the incense burning, the King and his fourfold army all ascended into the void. In the Heaven of the Thirty-three (Sudharmā), there is an incense called "Pure Adornment" (Vimalavyūha);
if one burns a single pellet and fumigates [the air], it causes the hearts of all the devas to turn toward the Buddha.
In the Yāma Heaven, there is an incense called "Pure Treasury" (Vimalagarbha); if one burns and fumigates with it, the hosts of the Yāma Heaven gather at the abode of the Heavenly King.
They listen to the Dharma together. In the Tuṣita Heaven there is a fragrance called Sindhava;
if one pellet is burned, it rains down all manner of offering requisites everywhere to make offerings to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. In the Nirmāṇarati Heaven there is a fragrance called Manohara;
if one pellet is burned, for seven days it rains down all kinds of ornamental articles everywhere. (From the *Qīngliáng shūchāo*).
It is said: First, the analogy is for the incense of generating the bodhicitta; next is the incense of patience, which the fire of anger cannot burn;

third is the incense of diligence, by which the demonic armies retreat and disperse. Next, five [incenses] correspond in sequence to the incense of the fivefold Dharma-body: fourth is the incense of ethical discipline, which is easily understood;
fifth is the incense of meditative concentration, through which one attains the stainless samādhi; sixth is the incense of wisdom, by which the king and his fourfold army all ascend into the air.
1. The fragrance of wisdom-realization, because it realizes emptiness. 2. The fragrance of liberation, because the mind recollects the Buddha and is thus freed from the five desires. 3.

The fragrance of knowledge and vision, because those who gather like clouds to hear the Dharma possess such knowledge and vision. 4. The fragrance that accords with the dharma-realm, *sindhuva* (salt).

One name has four realities; this [incense] should be used with salt because its fragrance resembles it. The tenth is "Fragrance that Forgets Subject and Object," hence it is named "Captivating the Mind.
The Dharma-body fragrance of the present Buddha, which possesses all merits, is likewise so.
II. A Brief Account of One’s Own Cultivation (in two parts): A. Self-Benefit.
"In my original ground, by means of the mind of mindfulness of the Buddha, I entered the patience of non-arising.
[Commentary] "Original" refers to the cause; "non-arising" refers to the fruit. The second phrase penetrates the fruit and encompasses the cause.

As for "mind," this describes my own mindfulness of the Buddha: it is not a recollection performed by the discriminating consciousness, but rather the total integration of the six sense faculties into a single, undisturbed mind.
It is mindfulness; it is entry into realization; it is patience and wisdom. "Non-arising" (*anutpāda*) is spoken of in terms of the principle of nature (*dharmatā*).
Because the mind of wisdom dwells in this principle of non-arising, it is called "patience with non-arising" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). As the *Qingliang shu* states:

"If one refers to the patience regarding the principle of non-arising, it is the patience of non-arising; if one refers to the wisdom of non-arising and the non-arising of afflictions, then non-arising itself is patience."

The nature of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharmatā) is without distinction from beginning to end; yet the stages of realization and entry into the patience regarding dharmas (dharma-kṣānti-bhūmi) are not equal.

The third fascicle of the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra* states: "This person immediately attains the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi-sūtra* (or *Śraddhābalādhāna-sūtra*) states:
"The dharma of the patience regarding non-arising can purify the first stage, the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), and one thereby attains great fearlessness and the place of peace and security."

It means that a bodhisattva gives rise to such a thought: "Because I have already attained abiding in the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), I give rise to a mind of peace and security;
in order to cause others to abide in the patience of non-arising, I arouse a mind of consolation. The *Ratnarāśi-sūtra* (Renwang jing) states:

"The Bodhisattva of the Patience of Non-arising refers to the wisdom of distant, immovable contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). "Distant" refers to the seventh stage, the Ground of Far-reaching Practice (*dūraṃgamā-bhūmi*); "immovable" refers to the [eighth stage].

The eighth stage is the Ground of Ninefold Skillful Wisdom (*navavidhā suvimalā buddhi-bhūmi*). Thus, one should know that this patience (*kṣānti*) begins with the three gradual stages and culminates in Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
For now, it is explained in terms of Equal Enlightenment, because the rank of Śrī-Ārya (Aśvaghosa) occupies the position of the Future Buddha (*upapadya-bodhisattva*).

The preceding phrase refers to the capacity for cultivation and realization; this phrase refers to what is realized through awakening—that is, using true, pure mindfulness to eliminate false, delusory turbidity.

Regarding perception (*saṃjñā*): when internal perceptions do not arise, external objects are naturally quiescent; internal and external phenomena are empty, and all things are without arising. The *Renwang jing* states:

"When all phenomena are empty, one attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Furthermore, this patience of non-arising is also termed the patience of non-extinction and the patience of non-abiding.
The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* says: "One who possesses the patience of non-arising does not perceive even the slightest phenomenon as arising, nor do they perceive [it as ceasing]."
A small portion of phenomena ceases. Why is this? If there is no arising, then there is no ceasing. If there is neither arising nor ceasing, then there is no abiding.

this is the perfection of giving (52). Single-mindedly reciting the Buddha’s name so that all evils naturally cease; this is the perfection of precepts (53). Single-mindedly...

The mind becomes naturally supple through mindfulness of the Buddha; this is the perfection of patience (54). Mindfulness of the Buddha with single-minded focus, never regressing; this is the perfection of vigor (55).
Mindfulness of the Buddha with single-minded focus, so that no other thoughts arise; this is the perfection of meditation (56).

Mindfulness of the Buddha with single-minded focus, such that right wisdom is clearly manifest; this is the perfection of wisdom (57). Mindfulness of the Buddha with single-minded focus, resulting in the attainment of perfect universal knowledge; this is Bodhi.

(58) Mindfully recollecting the Buddha with single-mindedness is the eternal, blissful, pure, and self-natured *nirvāṇa*. (59) Mindfully recollecting the Buddha as quiescent is the empty *tathāgatagarbha*.
(60) Mindfully recollecting the Buddha through mental visualization is the non-empty *tathāgatagarbha*. (61) Mindfully recollecting the Buddha through universal penetration.
62. The emptiness and non-emptiness of the *tathāgatagarbha*. 63. Mindfulness of the Buddha at sunrise: the time of initial illumination. 64. Mindfulness of the Buddha at mealtime:
the beginning of further illumination. 65. Mindfulness of the Buddha at midday: the middle of further illumination. 66. Mindfulness of the Buddha at dusk:
the end of further illumination. 67. Mindfulness of the Buddha at sunset: the time of returning illumination. 68. Mindfulness of the Buddha external to the mind.
(68) To contemplate the Buddha within the mind is the Initial Teaching (Śakyadeśanā). (69) To contemplate that the Buddha is the very mind is the Final Teaching (Nisthādeśanā).
(70) To contemplate that there is no Buddha apart from the mind is the Sudden Teaching (Aksaṇadeśanā). (71) To contemplate the universally integrated Buddha is the Perfect Teaching (Pūrṇadeśanā).

(72) Where there is a Buddha and a mind, with pure mindfulness succeeding one another, this is the phenomenal realm (Dharmadhātu). (73) Where there is neither Buddha nor mind, requiring no expedient means—this is the ultimate reality.

74. The Dharma-realm of Principle (*li-fajie*): through mindfulness of the Buddha and mindfulness of the mind, one enters the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). 75. The Dharma-realm of the Non-obstruction between Phenomena and Principle (*shi-li wuai fajie*):
whether it be the Buddha or the mind, they universally encompass the inexhaustible. 76. The Dharma-realm of the Non-obstruction between Phenomena and Phenomena (*shi-shi wuai fajie*):

a single gate of mindfulness of the Buddha encompasses infinite meanings; this is the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*). 77. The four or five gates of meaning are not limited to a single gate of mindfulness of the Buddha.
Distinct characteristics (78): The sixteen contemplations equally constitute mindfulness of the Buddha. Common characteristics (79): The purity of the environment is not the primary adornment.
Diverse characteristics (80): The single gate of mindfulness of the Buddha encompasses all meanings to achieve completion.

Characteristics of fulfillment (81): The fourfold and fivefold [categories] each abide in their own positions. Characteristics of disintegration (82): Mindfulness of the merits of the environment and the person.
The Buddha further encompasses all; this is the Gate of Simultaneous Fulfillment and Correspondence (83). Pervasively encompassing all phenomena without departing from mindfulness of the Buddha;
this is the Gate of Unobstructed Freedom between the Broad and the Narrow (84). Mindfulness of the Buddha through a single faculty gathers all six faculties;
this is the Gate of the Mutual Inclusion of One and Many Without Confusion (85). The Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha is itself all phenomena; this is the characteristic of all phenomena.
This is the Gate of Sovereignty (86). At the very moment of recollecting the Buddha, other gates do not appear; this is the Gate of the Simultaneous Accomplishment of Secrecy and Manifestation (87).
This gate of recollecting the Buddha universally encompasses all; this is the Gate of the Microscopic Containment and Stable Establishment of All Things (88).
The five types of recollecting the Buddha mutually encompass one another in infinite layers; this is the Gate of the Realm of Indra’s Net (89).
To see the gate of mindfulness of the Buddha is to see the inexhaustible; this is the gate of generating understanding by relying on phenomena to manifest the Dharma (90).

Mindfulness of the Buddha before and after is not different from the present mindfulness; this is the gate of the distinct formation of the ten periods of time (91). The single dharma of mindfulness of the Buddha encompasses inexhaustible dharmas;

this is the gate of the perfect clarity and fullness of virtues through the principal and its attendants (92). To mindfully contemplate the Buddha of one’s own mind is original enlightenment (*prakṛti-āśraya*).
(93) Mindfulness of the Buddha as the mind of faith: this is the stage of "name" within initial awakening. (94) Mindfulness of the Buddha as the mind of understanding:
this is the stage of "semblance" within initial awakening. (95) Mindfulness of the Buddha as the mind of realization: this is the stage of "partial realization" within initial awakening.

(96) Mindfulness of the Buddha as the attainment of Buddhahood: this is ultimate awakening. (97) At the time of mindfulness of the Buddha, one is tranquil and non-active: this is the Dharma-body Buddha. (98)
When one recollects the Buddha, there is no virtue that is not fully possessed; this is the Reward Body (Sambhogakāya) Buddha.

(99) When one recollects the Buddha, both ordinary beings and sages rejoice together; this is the Transformation Body (Nirmāṇakāya) Buddha. (100) Therefore, know that the single practice of nianfo encompasses all dharmas.
△ Second, the dedication of merit through taking refuge.
I prostrate to Śākyamuni Buddha and Amitābha Buddha, And to Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, and all the holy sages.
I look up with aspiration to the power of the grace bestowed by the Triple Gem, To cause this commentary on the sutra to pervade all lands throughout the dust-motes of the universe.
Seeing, hearing, rejoicing, and upholding or proclaiming [this teaching], one will ultimately attain birth in the Land of Peace and Bliss.
By dedicating this merit toward the entire Dharma-realm, may we together realize the fruit of unsurpassed Bodhi.
*The Commentary on the Chapter on Śrī Avalokiteśvara’s Perfect Penetration of Mindfulness of the Buddha from the Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, Scroll Lower (End).

Phonetic Glossary: *Vairocana* (this is translated as "Pervading All Places," and also as "Universal Radiance"). *Deng* (pronounced *zhèng*; the appearance of gazing straight ahead). *Méng* (pronounced *mēng*; to be dazed, confused, and lacking clarity).

*Pāri-jātaka* (this is translated as "Round-Born," referring to the tree of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; when its flowers bloom, their fragrance pervades fifty *yojanas*. It is also translated as "Variegated Adornment," because it is adorned all around with various colors of flowers interspersed and arrayed).

The fragrance of the clouds pervades the roots, stems, branches, leaves, bark, and fruits, such that there is nothing that is not fragrant. *Campaka* (pronounced *zhānbù*; this means "yellow flower")—its scent is most exquisite and its shape resembles the *jizi* flower;
its tree is tall and large. *Malaya* (translated as "High Mountain," or "Ox-Head," or "Stainless"). *Anavatapta* (this is the name of the "Lake Without Heat or Affliction").

*Arūṇa* (translated here as "also color and fragrance"). *Rākṣasa* (translated here as "swift demon," or "fearsome and violent"). *Suyāma* (translated here as "good time"; so called because they sing of wondrous goodness at the proper times). *Tuṣita* (in the language of China, "Contentment";

so called because they know satisfaction regarding the five objects of desire). *Saindhava* (translated here as "rock salt"; its fragrance resembles that [of the aforementioned], and salty water, horses, and vessels are all called *saindhava*;

it should here be understood as "salty"). *Lóngzhōng* (the appearance of old age and infirmity; meaning that as one grows old, the waist bends and the back stoops, like the curved bell of a dragon). *Ā* (sickness).

(Āpíng; *Laṅkā*, here translated as "The Mountain Unapproachable," where the Buddha preached this work, hence it is called the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*; *Arhat*, translated as "One of No-Birth," "Worthy of Offerings," or "Slayer of Foes," referring to the fourth fruit).

*Srotāpanna* (translated as "Stream-enterer," the first fruit). *Pratyutpanna* (translated as "Buddha-standing Constant-Walking Samādhi"). *Huáng* (pronounced *wàng*; meaning the mind has no leisure). *Liàng* (pronounced *liàng*; meaning a vehicle).

Nalakūvara (in the language of China, "Without Poverty," also translated as "As One Wishes"). The two faculties of the floating and the supreme (referring to the *bhrūṣa-rūpa-indriya* and the *paramārtha-indriya*; each of the six faculties possesses these two types).

*Diào* (pronounced *tiáo*; to sway or move). *Níhuán* (i.e., *nìpán*; a phonetic shift; this is translated as "entering extinction"). The eighteen *dhātus* (the six sense organs, the six objects, and the six consciousnesses).
*Jìngfàn* (Sanskrit: *Śuddhodana*; also translated as "True Purity" or "Pure White King," the name of the king). *Zhé* (pronounced *zhí*; identical to *zhé*). *Bū* (pronounced *bǔ*;
the hour of the monkey, the afternoon). *Indrājāla* (this is called the "Net of the Heavenly Emperor").

Among all practices for cultivation, the recitation of the Buddha’s name (*nien-fo*) is supreme. Regarding the methods for reciting the Buddha’s name, none surpass this sutra. Thus, the composition of these commentaries and sub-commentaries was unavoidable.
In the winter of the Wu-wu year, Mr. Dai Fuqi of Jingzhao, his eldest son Renchang, offered their preliminary congratulations.

My late father established a Huayan Assembly for his longevity. At that time, I was leading the assembly in the recitation of the "Contemplation of the Buddha" section from the *Cloud of Virtue* chapter.
As I examined it with deep concentration and contemplation, that night I dreamed that my late teacher, the Abbot, was lecturing on the "Avalokiteśvara" chapter.

By dawn, I had minutely studied Chengguan’s sub-commentary (*Shuchao*), and thus on the eighth day of the twelfth month, I began the exposition, which continued until the Lantern Festival of the year Jihwei (1759), and finally concluded in the fifth month of summer.
In the seventh month of this year, on the full moon, Master Fuqi Dai instructed me to immediately solicit donations for its carving.
I joyfully accepted his command. This may truly serve as a public warrant for the recovery from illness, the prolongation of life, and the increase of longevity and merit;
it is sufficient proof of these benefits. The carver said: "Is this the protection of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas? Or is it not?"
"Bodhisattva, what do you think? I replied, "You should know that the meaning of this sutra is inconceivable, and its karmic fruit and retribution are likewise inconceivable.
Why is this so? For it may reveal the pleasures of the five desires, or elucidate the realms of the six sense-objects;

it may serve as the arrow and shaft for fame and reputation, or tie together the causes and conditions for worldly production. Thus, such gifts and provisions are fundamentally harmful and without benefit."

Now, if one offers this Dharma-gate of Mindfulness of the Buddha for a single person, there is the benefit for that one person; if one offers it for ten million people, there is the benefit for those ten million people.
If it is offered at a single time and in a single place, there is benefit for that time and place;

if it extends throughout all sand-grain-like worlds until the end of the future, there is benefit for every dust mote of space across billions of kalpas. Thus, its power is equal to that of Śrī-ghoṣa, and its vows may be compared to those of Amitābha.
He gathers those who practice the mindfulness of the Buddha and leads them back to the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang). His merit, being free from outflows (anāsrava), is equal to empty space;

how could it be fathomed by the mind or discussed in words? Furthermore, since he has attained the Buddha-mind and ensured that the Triple Gem remains forever present, if the Buddha does not protect him, who else would?
Therefore, there is no need to doubt these signs of his humble and lowly status. The assembly agreed with this and requested that he compose a written account.
I exhorted the world to universally arouse the faith of all people. Upon hearing this, Master Mr. Weng said, "This matter is obscure and vague; there is no need to raise it so hastily.
Since the conditions for faith are already present among the masses, what is the point of extensive exhortation?

I replied, "It is not so. Birth and death are a great matter of life. How could the Dharma-gate that can liberate one from them be considered minor? Though those who have faith may be many, none are yet able to..."
This [teaching] is eternally pervasive; I now set it forth to manifest it. May those who have not yet believed be led to believe, and may those who already believe be led to increase their faith.
Furthermore, what harm is there in encouraging others to turn toward it? Thus, I have recorded this at the end of the commentary (*shūchō*) as an aid for its circulation.
Written on the eleventh day of the tenth month of the Gengshen year of the Kangxi era by the consecrated practitioner (Ganjing Xingzhe) Xu Fa.
